cards.title: The prince who saw old age
cards.text: Legend says Prince Siddhartha grew up shielded from suffering. Outside the palace he saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic. He left home.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: The legend of the Four Sights, from traditional biographies of the Buddha
cards.more:
Siddhartha Gautama lived in what’s now Nepal and northern India, probably around the 5th century BC, though scholars disagree on the dates. The four sights are legend, but they capture Buddhism’s starting question: if ageing, illness and death come for everyone, how should we live?

After years of extreme self-denial that nearly killed him, he’s said to have found a middle way and reached awakening while meditating under a tree. ‘Buddha’ means ‘awakened one’.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: A diagnosis in four steps
cards.text: The Buddha’s first teaching reads like a doctor’s diagnosis. Life involves dukkha, or suffering. Its cause is craving. It can end. And there’s a path to ending it.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
cards.more:
These are the Four Noble Truths, said to be the subject of the Buddha’s first sermon, given to five former companions in a deer park at Sarnath, near Varanasi.

Dukkha is usually translated as suffering, but it’s broader. It covers the stress of wanting things to be other than they are, and the background itch of dissatisfaction even when life is going fine.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 334 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
The second truth names the cause of suffering: taṇhā, which literally means ‘thirst’, and Müller keeps that image. Craving here is a restless reaching that never settles. Get the fruit, and your hand is already moving to the next branch.

The Buddha didn’t call wanting food or love evil. The trouble is clinging, needing things to be a certain way and suffering when they aren’t.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: ‘All created things perish,’ he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 277 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
Impermanence is the first of the three marks of existence. Everything that arises from causes, from moods to mountains, eventually passes. Müller’s ‘passive in pain’ means something like ‘no longer pushed around by suffering’.

The idea is that a lot of pain comes from treating changing things as permanent, like expecting a good moment to last forever or a bad one never to end.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: Look for the self in charge
cards.text: The Buddha asked listeners to look at their body, feelings, perceptions, mental habits and consciousness. All of them change. Which one is a permanent self? None, he said.
cards.em: Which one is a permanent self?
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Anattalakkhana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 22.59)
cards.more:
This is anattā, or not-self, traditionally the subject of the Buddha’s second sermon. It’s his hardest and most misunderstood idea. He wasn’t saying you don’t exist. What you call ‘me’, he said, is a process, a flowing bundle of changing parts, with no fixed thing hidden behind them.

It links back to craving. A lot of what we crave is protection for this imagined fixed self, its image and its need to be right.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.title: The middle way out
cards.text: Having tried palace luxury and near-starvation, the Buddha rejected both. His fourth truth is an eightfold path: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.
cards.author: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha)
cards.source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
cards.more:
The eight parts are traditionally grouped into three areas. Wisdom covers view and intention. Ethics covers speech, action and livelihood. Meditation covers effort, mindfulness and concentration.

‘Right’ here means something like skilful, not obedient. The parts work together like the spokes of a wheel, which is why an eight-spoked wheel became a symbol of Buddhism.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
cards.author: The Buddha
cards.source: Dhammapada, verse 1 (trans. F. Max Müller, 1881)
cards.more:
The Dhammapada, a collection of verses from the early Buddhist canon, opens with this line. The verse goes on: speak or act with an evil thought, and pain follows you the way the wheel follows the ox that pulls the cart.

The next verse is its mirror image. Act with a pure thought, and happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves. It’s a claim about cause and effect: habits of attention and intention shape what we experience.

thread.title: Buddhism in 7 cards

cards.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Teh King, chapter 11 (trans. James Legge, 1891)
cards.more:
The chapter goes on to clay pots and then to doors and windows. A pot holds things because it’s hollow. A room is useful because of the gaps cut into its walls.

Laozi’s point is that what isn’t there matters as much as what is. We notice the solid parts of things and overlook the emptiness that makes them work.

cards.text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout … the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Teh King, chapter 64 (trans. James Legge, 1891)
cards.more:
This is where the famous thousand-miles line comes from. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance, historically about a third of a mile. The chapter is about handling things while they’re small. Problems are easiest to fix early, and big things grow from humble starts.

Laozi’s stress is on the small and the early, because that’s where outcomes get decided. Tiny habits and minor warning signs both count.

cards.text: Yu, shall I teach you what knowledge is? … when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge.
cards.em: allow that you do not know
cards.author: Confucius
cards.source: Analects, Book 2.17 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
cards.more:
Yu was Zilu, one of Confucius’ most loyal and most impulsive disciples. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and conversations recorded by Confucius’ followers, and this one reads like a gentle correction for a student who liked to sound sure of himself.

Knowing where your knowledge ends counts as knowledge too. Socrates made a strikingly similar point in Athens a few generations later.

cards.text: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
cards.author: Confucius
cards.source: Analects, Book 7.21 (trans. James Legge, 1861)
cards.more:
Confucius was famous as a teacher, but he described himself first as a learner. In his view every companion is a lesson. Someone with a good quality shows you what to copy. Someone with a bad one shows you what to avoid, and maybe what to check for in yourself.

Elsewhere in the Analects he says that seeing someone fall short is a cue to turn inward and examine yourself.

cards.text: A good cook changes his chopper once a year,—because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,—because he hacks. But I have had this chopper nineteen years…
cards.author: Zhuangzi
cards.source: Chuang Tzu, chapter 3 (trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889)
cards.more:
In this story the cook of Prince Hui carves an ox so smoothly it looks like a dance. When the prince praises his skill, the cook explains that he no longer sees the whole animal. He follows its natural structure, sliding the blade through the gaps at the joints, so it never grinds against bone. After many thousand bullocks the edge still looks fresh from the whetstone.

The prince says the cook has taught him how to take care of his life.

cards.text: Arise! Awake! … The path is as sharp as a razor, impassable and difficult to travel, so the wise declare.
cards.author: Katha Upanishad
cards.source: Katha Upanishad, Part 3, verse 14 (trans. Swami Paramananda, 1919)
cards.more:
The Katha Upanishad tells of Nachiketas, a boy who goes to the house of Death and refuses to leave without learning what happens after we die. Death, impressed, teaches him about the deepest self, which he says is never born and never dies.

This verse is the wake-up call at the heart of that teaching. The full verse also says to seek out the Great Ones, illumined teachers. Somerset Maugham took the title of The Razor’s Edge from it.

cards.title: Doing by not forcing
cards.text: Wu wei, often translated ‘non-action’, means acting without force, the way water finds its path. Laozi says the Tao never forces anything, yet nothing is left undone.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Tao Te Ching, chapters 37 and 48
cards.more:
Wu wei is one of the core ideas of Taoism, and it doesn’t mean doing nothing. The Tao Te Ching contrasts the sage, who acts in tune with how things naturally unfold, with rulers and people who meddle and grasp, and so make things worse.

In modern terms it’s close to what psychologists call flow, full engagement without the feeling of strain. Over-managing a team or a child often backfires for the same reason.

cards.title: The child at the well
cards.text: Mencius said anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well feels instant alarm and compassion. That flash, he argued, shows everyone has the sprouts of goodness.
cards.author: Mencius
cards.source: Mencius, Book 2A.6
cards.more:
Mencius, a Confucian thinker of the 4th century BC, argued human nature is good. Not finished, but containing four ‘sprouts’: compassion, shame, respect and a sense of right and wrong. Like seedlings, they need tending and can be stunted by neglect. Nobody feels that alarm at the well to win the parents’ favour or the neighbours’ praise, he said.

The later Confucian Xunzi argued the opposite: people are bad by nature, and goodness has to be built through education and ritual.

cards.title: Keep a beginner’s mind
cards.text: Zen teacher Shunryu Suzuki warned that expertise quietly narrows the mind. The surer we are, the less we notice. He taught meeting even familiar things like a beginner.
cards.author: Shunryu Suzuki
cards.source: Zen Mind, Beginner’s Mind (1970)
cards.more:
Suzuki was a Japanese Soto Zen priest who moved to the United States and founded the San Francisco Zen Center, one of the most influential Zen communities in the West. His 1970 book Zen Mind, Beginner’s Mind, edited from informal talks, became one of the most popular introductions to Zen.

Beginner’s mind, shoshin in Japanese, means not letting what you know block what you could notice. Experts often miss things because they already know what to expect.

cards.title: Laozi may never have existed
cards.text: The Tao Te Ching is credited to Laozi, said to be an older contemporary of Confucius. Some modern scholars think he’s largely or wholly legendary.
cards.author: Laozi
cards.source: Wikipedia: Laozi
cards.more:
Laozi just means ‘Old Master’. The best-known legend has him tiring of a declining kingdom and heading west. At the frontier gate a guard named Yinxi recognised him and asked him to write down his wisdom first. The result, supposedly, was the Tao Te Ching.

Archaeology points to a messier story. Bamboo slips found at Guodian in 1993, dated to before 300 BC, hold early versions of parts of the text, which fits a book that grew over time.

cards.title: A tiny book, endlessly translated
cards.text: Only about 5,200 to 5,500 Chinese characters in 81 short chapters, yet the Tao Te Ching is among the most translated books ever, often ranked next to the Bible.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Tao Te Ching
cards.more:
It was first translated into a European language, French, in the early 19th century, and translators keep coming back. Part of the reason is the style: short, paradoxical lines with few grammatical markers, which leave a lot of room for interpretation. Two English versions of the same chapter can read like different poems.

Many ‘Lao Tzu quotes’ online are loose modern paraphrases, and some aren’t in the book at all. Older translations like James Legge’s are clunkier but closer to the text.

cards.title: Zen literally means meditation
cards.text: ‘Zen’ is the Japanese reading of the Chinese ‘Chan’, from the Sanskrit dhyāna, meaning meditation. It took shape in Tang dynasty China, mixing Indian Mahayana Buddhism with Taoist ideas.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Zen
cards.more:
The name is the whole programme. Zen puts meditation at the centre of practice, ahead of studying scriptures or performing rituals. From China it spread to Korea, where it’s called Seon, to Vietnam, where it’s Thiền, and to Japan.

The Taoist influence shows in Zen’s love of paradox, simplicity and nature, and its suspicion of explanations that get between you and direct experience. That mix later shaped Japanese gardens, tea ceremony and ink painting.

cards.title: Man or butterfly?
cards.text: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, then woke up. Was he a man who’d dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man?
cards.em: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly
cards.author: Zhuangzi
cards.source: Chuang Tzu, chapter 2 (trans. Herbert A. Giles, 1889)
cards.more:
Zhuangzi never settles it. He just notes there must be some difference between a man and a butterfly, and calls the shift between them a transformation.

It’s one of the most famous passages in Chinese philosophy. Descartes later worried he could never be completely sure he wasn’t dreaming, but Zhuangzi’s mood is different. He isn’t anxious about certainty. He enjoys the puzzle, and the lines between self and world, waking and dreaming, look less fixed to him than they feel.

cards.title: The sound of one hand
cards.text: You know the sound of two hands clapping. What is the sound of one hand?
cards.author: Hakuin Ekaku
cards.source: Koan devised by Hakuin Ekaku, 18th-century Japan
cards.more:
There’s no logical answer, by design. This koan comes from the Japanese Zen master Hakuin Ekaku, who in later life used it to stir up ‘great doubt’ in beginners. Koans are puzzles used in Zen training, especially in the Rinzai school, built so ordinary reasoning can’t crack them.

The aim is to wear out the habit of treating everything as a problem for the thinking mind. Students may work on one koan for months or years, presenting responses to a teacher.

cards.title: A free book from 868
cards.text: The oldest dated printed book is a Diamond Sutra from China, 868. Wang Jie paid for it on behalf of his parents, to be given away free.
cards.source: Diamond Sutra, British Library copy (Or.8210/P.2), dated 11 May 868
cards.more:
It was sealed for centuries in a cave library near Dunhuang, on the old Silk Road, until the explorer Aurel Stein bought it in 1907. It's now in the British Library.

Each page was carved backwards into its own block of wood. Woodblock printing was already old by then, which is why the scroll looks so polished. But a new book meant carving every page from scratch. The next step was carving single characters instead.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Bi Sheng's clay letters
cards.text: Around 1040, four centuries before Gutenberg, a Chinese commoner named Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay, one piece per character.
cards.source: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088); Wikipedia, Bi Sheng
cards.more:
He tried wood too, but it warped when it soaked up ink. We only know about him because the scholar Shen Kuo wrote the method down.

The type sat in an iron frame on a bed of warm wax and resin, and was warmed loose again afterwards and sorted for reuse. Shen Kuo noted it only paid off for big print runs. Chinese needs thousands of characters, so woodblocks stayed competitive for centuries.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Korea printed with metal first
cards.text: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is the Jikji, Buddhist teachings printed at a Korean temple in 1377. That's 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.
cards.source: UNESCO Memory of the World register (2001); Wikipedia, Jikji
cards.more:
It was printed at Heungdeok Temple. Korean printers cast their characters in bronze, which fixed the problem of clay and wood wearing out, and the royal court backed big printing projects in the next century.

Only the second volume survives. A French diplomat collected it in Seoul in the late 1800s, and it now sits in the Bibliotheque nationale de France in Paris. Korea has asked for it back for decades. UNESCO listed it in its Memory of the World register in 2001.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Forty-nine Gutenberg Bibles left
cards.text: Gutenberg finished his Bible in Mainz around 1455. He printed somewhere between 160 and 185 copies. Forty-nine survive in at least substantial part.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Gutenberg Bible
cards.more:
About three quarters were on paper and the rest on calfskin vellum. They're among the most valuable books on Earth.

Gutenberg didn't invent printing, or even movable type. He built a system that worked: a hand mould for casting identical metal letters fast, a metal that melted easily and set hard, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press adapted from wine and paper making. Then he went broke and lost his shop to his financial backer.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Twenty million books in fifty years
cards.text: In 1450 Gutenberg's shop in Mainz was Europe's only print shop. By 1500, presses in about 270 European cities had turned out more than 20 million copies.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Printing press (citing Buringh and van Zanden, 2009, and the British Library's Incunabula Short Title Catalogue)
cards.more:
By 1600 the running total was somewhere between 150 and 200 million. Printers travelled, many of them trained in Mainz, and set up wherever there was paper and money. Venice became the giant.

Books printed before 1501 are called incunabula, from the Latin for swaddling clothes, because print was still a baby. Prices fell, and scholars hundreds of miles apart could own the same edition and point to the same page.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Luther's 300,000 pamphlets
cards.text: Between 1518 and 1520, printers put about 300,000 copies of Martin Luther's writings into circulation. By around 1520 he was the most published author in Europe.
cards.em: the most published author in Europe
cards.source: Wikipedia, Printing press (citing Pettegree, Brand Luther, 2015)
cards.more:
Printers across Germany ran 291 editions of his 45 original works. The 95 Theses of 1517 were in Latin, for academic debate. What made him famous were short German pamphlets, cheap enough for ordinary townspeople.

Earlier reformers like Jan Hus had been silenced. Luther couldn't be, because by the time anyone tried to suppress a pamphlet, a dozen cities had reprinted it. The pope and secular rulers were caught off guard.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Identical copies changed science
cards.text: Elizabeth Eisenstein argued print's real gift was identical copies. With thousands of readers using the same star tables, errors got spotted and fixed in the next edition.
cards.author: Elizabeth Eisenstein
cards.source: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
cards.more:
Before print, every hand copy was a little different and added new mistakes. Scholars spent their energy trying to recover what the original said.

With fixed editions, knowledge could build up instead of slowly decaying. Astronomers compared the same tables, and anatomists corrected each other's drawings. Eisenstein's two-volume book from 1979 tied this to both the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution. Historians still argue about how far to push her thesis.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.text: …printing, gunpowder, and the compass. For these three have changed the appearance and state of the whole world…
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Novum Organum, Book 1, Aphorism 129 (1620), ed. Joseph Devey
cards.more:
Bacon wrote this in 1620, about 170 years after Gutenberg. He noted that all three were unknown to the ancients. He didn't know all three had roots in China.

Printing is a good example. It started with Tang dynasty woodblocks, moved to clay and then metal type in China and Korea, and became a mass system in Mainz. By Bacon's day it was feeding the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

thread.title: How printing changed the world (8 cards)

cards.title: Cleopatra and the Moon landing
cards.text: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. It went up around 2600 BC. She died in 30 BC.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Pyramid of Giza; Cleopatra
cards.more:
That's about 2,570 years from pyramid to Cleopatra, and about 2,000 from Cleopatra to Apollo 11 in 1969. Egyptian civilization ran for roughly three thousand years, so to her the pyramid was already deep antiquity.

She wasn't ethnically Egyptian either. She was a Ptolemy, from a Macedonian Greek dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals, and is said to be the first of her line to learn Egyptian.

cards.title: Oxford is older than the Aztecs
cards.text: Teaching at Oxford was going on by 1096. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, wasn't founded until 1325, and the Aztec Empire formed in 1428.
cards.source: Wikipedia, University of Oxford; Tenochtitlan
cards.more:
So when the Aztec Empire took shape, Oxford had been teaching for more than 300 years. The empire was short-lived too. The Spanish conquest destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521.

At its height the city, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was one of the largest in the world. Mexico City stands on its ruins. Oxford has no exact founding date. It got a boost in 1167, when Henry II banned English students from studying at the University of Paris.

cards.title: Napoleon was average height
cards.text: Napoleon was recorded as 5 feet 2, but in French inches, which were longer. That's about 1.67 metres, close to average for a Frenchman of his day.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Napoleon complex
cards.more:
English readers saw 5 foot 2 and pictured a tiny man. British cartoonists, James Gillray especially, drew him as a tantrum-throwing little man, and the image stuck.

His nickname, le petit caporal, the little corporal, was a term of affection from his soldiers. He was also often surrounded by his Imperial Guard, who had minimum height requirements. So the Napoleon complex is named after a man who wasn't short.

cards.title: No horns on Viking helmets
cards.text: No evidence says Vikings wore horned helmets. That look is a 19th-century invention, spread by Wagner's operas. Surviving Viking helmets are plain iron caps.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Horned helmet
cards.more:
The best-preserved Viking-age helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway in 1943, is a simple iron cap with a spectacle-like guard around the eyes. Horns would just give an enemy's blade something to catch.

Horned helmets did exist in Scandinavia, but much earlier, in the Bronze Age, and seem to have been ceremonial. Costumes for the first Bayreuth staging of Wagner's Ring cycle in 1876 helped fix the image.

cards.title: Columbus and the round Earth
cards.text: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round. The myth that Columbus had to convince them came later, notably from Washington Irving's 1828 biography.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Myth of the flat Earth
cards.more:
Roundness had been accepted since the ancient Greeks, and a popular medieval textbook was called On the Sphere. The real fight over Columbus was about size. His critics said the Earth was too big to reach Asia by sailing west. They were right. He'd badly underestimated the distance, and survived only because an unknown continent was in the way.

The myth spread in the 1800s partly because it suited a story of science battling religious ignorance. Historians see that story as heavily exaggerated.

cards.text: ...right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
cards.em: the weak suffer what they must
cards.author: Thucydides
cards.source: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, the Melian Dialogue (c. 400 BC), trans. Richard Crawley
cards.more:
In 416 BC Athens sent a fleet to Melos, a small island that wanted to stay neutral in the war with Sparta. Thucydides gives these words to the Athenian envoys. They don't claim justice. They point at their power.

The Melians appealed to fairness and the gods, and hoped Sparta would help. It didn't. Athens took the island, killed the men and enslaved the women and children. The dialogue is still taught as the founding text of political realism.

cards.text: His reign is marked by the rare advantage of furnishing very few materials for history … little more than the register of the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind.
cards.em: crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind
cards.author: Edward Gibbon
cards.source: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Vol. 1, ch. 3 (1776)
cards.more:
Gibbon is talking about Antoninus Pius, Roman emperor from 138 to 161 AD. A good reign leaves historians almost nothing to write about, because history mostly records disasters.

The second half often gets quoted alone as a gloomy verdict on humanity. In context it's nearly a compliment. Peace and quiet prosperity don't make dramatic events, so the long stretches when things went fine, where most people actually lived, barely leave a trace.

cards.text: ...in peace the sons bury their fathers, but in war the fathers bury their sons.
cards.author: Herodotus
cards.source: The Histories, Book 1, ch. 87 (c. 430 BC), trans. G. C. Macaulay
cards.more:
Herodotus gives the line to Croesus, the rich king of Lydia, after Cyrus the Great of Persia has taken his empire. Before attacking Persia, Croesus asked the oracle at Delphi. It said that if he went to war, a great empire would be destroyed. It was his own.

When Cyrus asks who talked him into the war, Croesus blames the god of the Greeks, then adds this.

cards.title: Did wheat domesticate us?
cards.text: Early farmers worked longer and ate worse than foragers, Yuval Noah Harari argues. The payoff was more people. In his telling, wheat used us.
cards.author: Yuval Noah Harari
cards.source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, ch. 5 (English edition, 2014)
cards.more:
In his version, wheat used us to spread across the planet as much as we used it. Harari separates a species' success from individual wellbeing. Counted in copies, wheat and humans both won big. Counted in hours of toil, back problems and tooth decay, many early farmers lost.

People didn't go back because each step seemed sensible at the time, and once populations depended on harvests there was no route back to foraging. He calls it a trap, where luxuries turn into necessities. Not every archaeologist agrees with his framing.

cards.title: Eurasia runs east to west
cards.text: Geography decided who conquered whom, Jared Diamond argues. Eurasia runs east to west, so crops spread across similar climates. The Americas and Africa run north to south.
cards.author: Jared Diamond
cards.source: Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997)
cards.more:
Running north to south means crossing climate zones, which slowed farming down. Diamond started from a question a New Guinean politician named Yali asked him: why did Europeans end up with so much cargo?

His answer is a chain. Eurasia had more wild plants and big animals that could be domesticated. Farming brought surpluses, dense populations and states. Living near livestock bred epidemics, and immunity. In the Americas, germs killed far more people than guns. Critics say he downplays culture and chance.

cards.title: From the Trojan horse to Vietnam
cards.text: Barbara Tuchman called it folly: governments pursuing policies against their own interest, even when warned at the time. Her examples run from the Trojan horse to Vietnam.
cards.author: Barbara Tuchman
cards.source: The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (1984)
cards.more:
Her test was strict. Looking foolish in hindsight didn't count. People at the time had to see the danger and say so, and a workable alternative had to exist. The policy also had to outlast any one ruler.

Her cases include the Renaissance popes, whose corruption helped provoke the Reformation, and British ministers who kept provoking the American colonies despite warnings in Parliament. She called the root problem wooden-headedness, sticking to a fixed idea while ignoring the evidence.

cards.title: Mammoths or pyramids?
cards.text: Which came first: the last woolly mammoths, or the Great Pyramid of Giza?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Woolly mammoth
cards.more:
The pyramid. It went up around 2600 BC, and the last known woolly mammoths lived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia in the Arctic Ocean, until about 4,000 years ago, around 2000 BC.

Most mammoths had vanished from the mainland by about 10,000 years ago, but small island groups hung on. One on St. Paul Island in Alaska lasted until about 5,600 years ago, and the Wrangel mammoths outlived it by more than a thousand years.

cards.title: Born the same day
cards.text: Two men who reshaped the 19th century were born on 12 February 1809, one in a Kentucky log cabin, one in a well-off English home. Who were they?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Charles Darwin; Abraham Lincoln
cards.more:
Abraham Lincoln and Charles Darwin. Lincoln was born in a one-room cabin in Hardin County, Kentucky. Darwin was born in Shrewsbury, England, into a wealthy family of doctors and industrialists.

Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. Lincoln was elected president in 1860 and issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. Both hated slavery. Darwin saw it firsthand in Brazil on the Beagle voyage and wrote about it with disgust.

cards.title: The man who memorised nonsense
cards.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus learned nonsense syllables like WID and ZOF and tested his recall. Forgetting was steep at first, then slowed. Much was gone in a day or two.
cards.em: gone in a day or two
cards.source: Hermann Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1885)
cards.more:
He did this in the 1880s and used nonsense on purpose, so meaning and prior knowledge couldn't help. He was his only subject, a real limitation, but a 2015 replication by Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros found a very similar curve.

Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense, so his exact percentages aren't gospel. The shape holds: a steep loss early, then a long, slow tail. The next cards cover what slows it down.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Spacing won 259 of 271
cards.text: A 2006 review compared spaced study with cramming, same total time. Spacing won in 259 of 271 comparisons. Few findings in learning research are this reliable.
cards.source: Cepeda et al., Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin (2006)
cards.more:
Ebbinghaus noticed the spacing effect himself, and it has replicated for well over a century, across ages, subjects and even other species.

Why it works is still debated. One idea: letting a memory fade a little before you revisit it forces harder recall, which strengthens it more. The best gap depends on how long you need to remember. Later work by Cepeda and colleagues suggests very roughly 10 to 20 percent of that time, shrinking proportionally for longer horizons.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Rereaders won for five minutes
cards.text: Students either reread a passage or took practice tests on it. After five minutes, rereaders did slightly better. After a week, testers remembered far more.
cards.source: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science (2006)
cards.more:
It's called the testing effect, or retrieval practice. Pulling something out of memory changes the memory and makes it easier to find next time.

It works best with spacing, and with feedback so mistakes don't stick. It even helps when you fail to recall, as long as you check the answer after. Closing the book and writing down what you remember counts. So does answering a flashcard out loud before flipping it.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Learning painters by shuffling them
cards.text: People learned painters' styles one artist at a time, or shuffled together. Shuffling did better at recognising new paintings. Most people still believed one-at-a-time had helped more.
cards.author: Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork
cards.source: Learning Concepts and Categories, Psychological Science (2008)
cards.more:
Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork ran this in 2008. Shuffling is called interleaving, and it makes you notice what makes each thing different. Doug Rohrer and colleagues found the same in maths: students who practised mixed problem sets did much better on later tests, because they had to work out which method each problem needed.

Interleaving feels slower and messier, and early performance looks worse. That's a big part of why people avoid it.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Why easy studying fools you
cards.text: Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties: spacing, testing and mixing feel clumsy but make learning last. Rereading feels smooth, and we mistake that smoothness for mastery.
cards.em: we mistake that smoothness for mastery
cards.author: Robert A. Bjork
cards.source: Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings, in Metacognition (1994)
cards.more:
We judge learning by how fluent it feels. Rereading makes a chapter familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. But recognising something on the page is very different from producing it on a blank sheet.

Not every difficulty is desirable. Bjork's point is that a difficulty helps when it makes you do the mental work you'll need later, like recalling and telling things apart. Confusing explanations or background noise are just hard.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.text: …without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again … Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them.
cards.author: Benjamin Franklin
cards.source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, part one (written 1771)
cards.more:
As a teenager, Franklin taught himself to write by rebuilding essays from The Spectator. He jotted short hints, waited a few days, rewrote the essay without looking, then compared his version with the original and fixed his mistakes.

He varied it too. He turned some essays into verse and later back into prose to stretch his vocabulary. He also jumbled his notes, then tried to restore their order, to learn how to structure an argument.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.title: Make It Stick, boiled down
cards.text: Make It Stick boils decades of learning research into a few habits. Quiz yourself instead of rereading. Space reviews out. Mix topics. Try answering before you're taught.
cards.author: Peter C. Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel
cards.source: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning (2014)
cards.more:
Put together: after a lecture or chapter, close it and write what you remember. Check against the source and note the gaps, like Franklin. Review a few days later, then a week after that, mixing in older material.

The authors, Peter Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel, also stress calibration: use tests to find out what you actually know. Most people who try it discover they knew less than they thought.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

cards.text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Essays, 'Of Studies' (1625 edition)
cards.more:
In Bacon's English, conference means conversation and debate, and exact means precise. Reading stocks your mind. Talking with others makes you quick with what you know. Writing pins vague ideas down, because a sentence on paper can't hide behind a feeling of understanding.

Many people only find out they don't understand something when they try to explain it in writing and get stuck halfway.

cards.text: As the art of reading … is the art of skipping, so the art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 2, ch. 22 'Reasoning' (1890)
cards.more:
James is describing how expert thinking works. As you get better at something, you stop processing every detail and see only the features that matter. A strong chess player glances at a board and ignores most of it. A beginner has to consider every piece.

Skimming to find what matters, then reading that part slowly, is a skill. The hard part is choosing what to overlook, and that depends on knowing what you're after.

cards.text: …to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.
cards.em: into as many parts as possible
cards.author: René Descartes
cards.source: Discourse on the Method, part II (1637; trans. John Veitch)
cards.more:
Descartes set himself four rules for thinking. Accept nothing as true that you don't clearly know. Break each difficulty into parts. Work from the simplest parts up. Review everything so nothing is left out. This is the second.

'Write the report' is paralysing. 'List the five sections' isn't. The phrase 'as might be necessary' matters: the aim is to keep splitting until each piece is something you can actually do or answer.

cards.text: People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, no. 10 (1670; trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Telling someone an answer, however clearly, hands them a conclusion with no roots. Helping them find it gives them a path back to it.

Learning research points the same way. The generation effect, studied since the 1970s, shows that information you produce yourself, even from small cues, is remembered better than information you just read. In the pensée before this one, Pascal adds a tip: to correct someone, first find the side from which they're right and admit it.

cards.title: The man with a hammer
cards.text: Charlie Munger said isolated facts are nearly useless without a latticework of big ideas from many fields. Know only one, and every problem looks like a nail.
cards.em: every problem looks like a nail
cards.author: Charlie Munger
cards.source: A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom, talk at USC Business School (1994)
cards.more:
His examples of models included compound interest, incentives, feedback loops and margin of safety. Problems don't arrive sorted into academic departments. A business problem can be part psychology and part maths.

Munger suggested learning the big ideas from each major field well enough to use them, then checking a problem against several. He reckoned around 80 or 90 important models do most of the work.

cards.title: Invert, always invert
cards.text: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid that. Charlie Munger took the habit from the mathematician Carl Jacobi.
cards.author: Charlie Munger
cards.source: Commencement speech at the Harvard School, Los Angeles (1986)
cards.more:
In a 1986 graduation speech, Munger described a good life by listing sure routes to a miserable one, like envy, resentment and unreliability. Our minds spot what's clearly wrong faster than they design what's ideal. Ask how to make a team miserable and answers come fast: unclear priorities, surprise deadlines.

Jacobi used the idea in maths, where attacking a problem from its converse or negation often makes it easier. Proof by contradiction is the same move.

cards.title: The cost of a quick check
cards.text: Switch tasks and part of your mind stays on the last one. Sophie Leroy calls it attention residue. Even a quick inbox check leaves some.
cards.author: Cal Newport
cards.source: Deep Work, part 1 (2016)
cards.more:
In Leroy's 2009 experiments, people who left one task unfinished and moved to another did worse on the second, because their thoughts kept drifting back.

Cal Newport builds on this in Deep Work. He argues that focusing without distraction on hard tasks is getting rarer just as it gets more valuable. His fixes are structural: schedule focus blocks in advance, batch shallow work like email, and treat focus as a skill that weakens without use.

cards.title: A good bet can still lose
cards.text: Former poker champion Annie Duke calls it resulting: judging a decision by how it turned out. A drunk driver who gets home safely still made a bad choice.
cards.author: Annie Duke
cards.source: Thinking in Bets, ch. 1 (2018)
cards.more:
Her fix is to judge the decision separately from the outcome. What did you know at the time, and how did you weigh the odds? Learning only from outcomes means learning the wrong lessons from luck.

She opens her book with the pass at the end of the 2015 Super Bowl that was intercepted and instantly branded one of the worst calls ever. It would have been praised if it had worked, and a close look at the odds suggests it was defensible.

cards.title: Growth mindset, smaller than advertised
cards.text: Carol Dweck's research suggests people who see ability as something that grows handle setbacks better. Large recent studies say the effect on school results is real but modest.
cards.author: Carol Dweck
cards.source: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)
cards.more:
Dweck contrasts a fixed mindset, where failure shows your limits, with a growth mindset, where failure tells you what to practise next. Praising effort and strategy instead of talent was one of her best-known recommendations.

The evidence got more nuanced. A 2018 meta-analysis found weak overall links between mindset and achievement. A large 2019 US national study found a short online mindset lesson raised grades slightly, mostly for lower-achieving students.

cards.title: Everyone's thesis took longer
cards.text: Psychology students guessed their senior theses would take about 34 days. Even their worst-case guesses averaged under 49. The real average was 55.5 days.
cards.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1994)
cards.more:
That was a 1994 study, and only about 30% finished within the time they'd predicted. Kahneman and Tversky named this the planning fallacy in 1979. We plan by picturing the steps going roughly as intended, and underweight the dull fact that they rarely do.

The best-known fix is reference class forecasting. Start from how long similar projects actually took, for you or others, then adjust a little for what's genuinely different.

cards.title: Chesterton's fence
cards.text: Chesterton's reformer finds a fence across a road, sees no use for it, and wants it gone. A wiser one says: first find out why it's there.
cards.em: first find out why it's there
cards.author: G. K. Chesterton
cards.source: The Thing, 'The Drift from Domesticity' (1929)
cards.more:
G. K. Chesterton wrote this in 1929. Rules and habits often exist because of a problem nobody remembers anymore, precisely because the fence solved it. Remove it and the problem can come back.

That doesn't mean every fence is wise. The burden is to understand before removing, and often the reason is long gone and the fence can go.

cards.title: Can you really multitask?
cards.text: Plenty of people say they're good at doing several things at once. What's actually happening in your head when you think you're multitasking?
cards.source: Monsell, Task switching, Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2003)
cards.more:
For anything that needs attention, you're mostly switching. Each switch costs something: in lab tasks, people are slower and make more errors right after changing tasks than after repeating one, even when warned a switch is coming.

Each cost is small, often a fraction of a second, but it adds up over a day of toggling and grows with harder tasks. The exception is pairing something automatic with something that needs thought, like walking while talking.

cards.title: Are you a visual learner?
cards.text: Most teachers and students believe people learn best in their preferred style: visual, auditory or hands-on. Does matching teaching to someone's style actually help?
cards.em: learn best in their preferred style
cards.source: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer & Bjork, Psychological Science in the Public Interest (2008)
cards.more:
There's no good evidence that it does. In 2008 a panel led by Harold Pashler set out what a proper test needs: sort learners by style, teach each group in more than one style, and check if each does best in its own. Very few studies did this, and those that did mostly found no such match.

People do have preferences, and some subjects suit some formats. Maps are visual. Music is auditory. The best format depends more on the content than the person.

cards.title: Is 10,000 hours the magic number?
cards.text: Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers made 10,000 hours of practice famous as the path to expertise. Is practice really what separates the best from everyone else?
cards.source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science (2014)
cards.more:
Partly. Practice matters a lot, but 10,000 isn't a rule. Anders Ericsson, whose violin research inspired the idea, said Gladwell oversimplified it: the figure was an average at one age, and the kind of practice mattered as much as the amount.

A 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara and colleagues found deliberate practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and under 1% in professions.

cards.title: Probability started with a gambler
cards.text: A gambler asked Blaise Pascal how to split a pot fairly when a game stops early. His letters with Pierre de Fermat laid the foundations of probability.
cards.source: Pascal-Fermat correspondence on the problem of points (1654)
cards.more:
This puzzle, from 1654, is the problem of points. Say two players race to win a set number of rounds, and the game stops when one needs 1 more win and the other needs 3. Pascal and Fermat looked forward: list every way the remaining rounds could go, and split the pot by each player's share of those futures.

The second player needs three wins in a row, a 1 in 8 chance, so a fair split is 7 to 1. That idea is the core of expected value.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: The birthday puzzle
cards.text: How many people need to be in a room for a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday?
cards.em: two of them share a birthday
cards.source: The birthday problem (assuming 365 equally likely birthdays)
cards.more:
Just 23. With 23 people the chance of a shared birthday is about 50.7%. With 70 it's over 99.9%.

Most guesses are far higher because we picture someone matching our own birthday. But any pair counts, and 23 people form 253 pairs. The neat way to calculate it is the chance that nobody matches: 365/365 × 364/365 × 363/365 and so on for 23 people, which comes to about 49.3%.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: Three doors, two goats
cards.text: You pick one of three doors. One hides a car, two hide goats. The host, who knows which is which, opens another door: goat. Should you switch?
cards.source: Marilyn vos Savant, 'Ask Marilyn', Parade (1990)
cards.more:
Yes. Switching wins two times in three. Your first pick is right one time in three, and the host's reveal doesn't change that. So the other closed door holds the car two times in three.

When Marilyn vos Savant gave this answer in 1990, about 10,000 readers wrote in, nearly 1,000 of them with PhDs, mostly to say she was wrong. Even Paul Erdős stayed unconvinced until he saw a computer simulation.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: How evidence should change your mind
cards.text: Bayes' theorem, in odds form: new odds = old odds × how much likelier the evidence is if the idea is true. Thomas Bayes's essay came out in 1763.
cards.author: Thomas Bayes
cards.source: An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances, Philosophical Transactions (1763)
cards.more:
Say something is a long shot at odds of 1 to 9, and you see evidence three times as likely if it's true. The odds become 3 to 9, which is 1 to 3, a 25% chance. So one piece of evidence can't make a rare thing likely on its own.

Bayes was an English minister and died before publishing. His friend Richard Price edited the essay and published it.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: You tested positive. How worried?
cards.text: A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test catches 90% of cases and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. You test positive. What's the chance you have it?
cards.source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction, Psychological Review (1995)
cards.more:
About 9%, not 90%. Take 1,000 people. Ten have the disease, and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 healthy people, about 89 test positive by mistake. That's 98 positives, and only 9 are real: roughly 1 in 11.

This is the base rate fallacy. The rarity of the disease outweighs the accuracy of the test. Gerd Gigerenzer and others found many doctors get this badly wrong with percentages, and far more often right with counts of people.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: Black came up 26 times
cards.text: A Monte Carlo roulette wheel landed on black 26 times in a row in 1913. Gamblers lost millions betting red was due. The wheel had no memory.
cards.source: Monte Carlo Casino (1913), the standard example of the gambler's fallacy
cards.more:
The gambler's fallacy is believing a random process will balance itself out in the short run. The law of large numbers says the share of black settles near its expected value over many spins. It gets there by drowning out streaks with more data. Nothing corrects them.

A run of 26 of one colour on a single-zero wheel has odds of about 1 in 68 million. Rare, but with enough wheels spinning for enough years, rare things happen somewhere.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.title: Out of how many?
cards.text: Gerd Gigerenzer blames most probability mistakes on how numbers are shown. Give people '9 out of 1,000' instead of '0.9%', and far more get the answer right.
cards.author: Gerd Gigerenzer
cards.source: Calculated Risks: How to Know When Numbers Deceive You (2002)
cards.more:
Gigerenzer calls this risk literacy and argues it can be taught, even to children, once numbers are shown as natural frequencies.

This thread as a checklist. Look forward at every possible outcome, like Pascal and Fermat. Expect coincidences, because many small chances add up. Ask what the person giving you information knows, like the Monty Hall host. Start from the base rate and update, like Bayes. And roulette wheels have no memory.

thread.title: Probability will fool you, in 7 cards

cards.text: Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty—a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture…
cards.em: not only truth, but supreme beauty
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: Mysticism and Logic, 'The Study of Mathematics' (1918; essay first published 1907)
cards.more:
Russell wrote this while working toward Principia Mathematica, an attempt to build maths from pure logic. For him the beauty was in a proof's certainty and economy: a few assumptions, a chain of steps, and a conclusion that couldn't be otherwise.

Mathematicians say the same about Euclid's proof that the primes never run out, or Euler's identity, which ties e, i, π, 1 and 0 together in one short line.

cards.text: Thus mathematics may be defined as the subject in which we never know what we are talking about, nor whether what we are saying is true.
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: Mysticism and Logic, 'Mathematics and the Metaphysicians' (1918; essay first published 1901)
cards.more:
It's a joke with a serious point. Russell is describing pure maths as logic: start from assumptions and deduce what follows, without caring whether the assumptions describe anything real. A proof says 'if these, then that'.

That's why maths is so reusable. The same theorems about abstract symmetry groups apply to crystals, Rubik's cubes and particle physics, because the maths never committed to what the objects were.

cards.text: At the moment when I put my foot on the step the idea came to me … that the transformations … were identical with those of non-Euclidean geometry.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, book I, ch. 3 'Mathematical Creation' (1908; trans. G. B. Halsted, 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré had worked hard on the problem for weeks, then left it for a geology trip. The answer came as he stepped onto a bus, in the middle of a conversation about something else. He checked it later, and it was right.

He saw a pattern: hard conscious work, a break, a sudden insight, then careful checking. The sudden part never came without the hard part. Psychologists call the break incubation, and studies suggest it helps with some creative problems.

cards.text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, book I, ch. 1 'The Choice of Facts' (1908; trans. G. B. Halsted, 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré goes on to say he doesn't mean the beauty of colours and appearances, but a deeper beauty that comes from the harmonious order of the parts. He argues this taste for simplicity and harmony steers scientists toward the facts and theories that turn out to matter.

Mathematicians still talk this way. An elegant proof is prized because it usually shows why something is true, as well as that it is.

cards.title: The primes never run out
cards.text: Euclid's proof: list every prime, multiply them, add 1. The result is prime or built from primes you missed. So no list is complete.
cards.author: Euclid
cards.source: Elements, book IX, proposition 20 (c. 300 BC)
cards.more:
Divide the new number by any prime on the list and you get remainder 1, so none of them divides it. The argument is about 2,300 years old.

A common misreading is that the product plus 1 is always prime. 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30,031, which is 59 × 509. The proof only needs some new prime, and neither 59 nor 509 was on the list.

cards.title: Some infinities are bigger
cards.text: Cantor proved no infinite list holds every real number. Change digit 1 of entry 1, digit 2 of entry 2, and so on. The result isn't on the list.
cards.em: The result isn't on the list
cards.author: Georg Cantor
cards.source: Über eine elementare Frage der Mannigfaltigkeitslehre (1891)
cards.more:
This diagonal argument, from 1891, means there are more real numbers than counting numbers. Before Cantor, infinity was just infinity. After him there was a hierarchy, with the countable infinity of 1, 2, 3 at the bottom.

The same trick later powered Gödel's incompleteness theorems and Turing's proof that some problems no computer can solve. Leopold Kronecker fiercely opposed Cantor. David Hilbert defended him: no one would drive mathematicians out of the paradise Cantor had created.

cards.title: Full hotel, room for more
cards.text: A hotel has infinitely many rooms, all full. A new guest arrives. Move everyone from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is free.
cards.author: David Hilbert
cards.source: Lecture 'Über das Unendliche' (1924-25); popularised in George Gamow, One Two Three... Infinity (1947)
cards.more:
Even infinitely many new guests fit: move everyone to room 2n and all the odd rooms open up. David Hilbert used the story to show how differently infinite sets behave. In an infinite hotel, the guests can be matched one-to-one with only some of the rooms.

There's one thing it can't do: give a room to one guest for every real number. That's Cantor's bigger infinity, and no room plan fits them all.

cards.title: Why energy is conserved
cards.text: Emmy Noether proved every continuous symmetry comes with a conservation law. If physics works the same tomorrow as today, energy is conserved.
cards.author: Emmy Noether
cards.source: Invariante Variationsprobleme (1918)
cards.more:
If the laws are the same here as over there, momentum is conserved. Before her 1918 theorem, conservation laws were facts found by experiment.

She did this while barred from a proper paid post at Göttingen because she was a woman. David Hilbert and Felix Klein brought her in to help with problems in Einstein's general relativity, and for a while her lectures had to be advertised under Hilbert's name.

cards.title: True but unprovable
cards.text: Kurt Gödel proved in 1931, in his mid-twenties, that any consistent set of axioms that can do basic arithmetic has true statements it can't prove.
cards.author: Kurt Gödel
cards.source: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems (1931)
cards.more:
His trick was to make arithmetic talk about itself. He encoded statements as numbers, then built one that says, roughly, 'this statement can't be proved in this system'. If the system is consistent, that statement is true and unprovable.

His second theorem says such a system can't prove its own consistency. Together they ended David Hilbert's hope for a complete, provably safe foundation for maths. They apply only to formal systems with precise rules.

cards.title: A rather dull taxi number
cards.text: Visiting Ramanujan in hospital, G. H. Hardy said his taxi's number, 1729, seemed rather dull. Ramanujan disagreed: it's the smallest number that's a sum of two cubes two ways.
cards.em: sum of two cubes two ways
cards.source: G. H. Hardy's recollection of a visit to Ramanujan in Putney, London (c. 1918)
cards.more:
1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. It wasn't a lucky guess: the number was already in one of his notebooks, and Frénicle de Bessy had noted it in 1657. Numbers like it are now called taxicab numbers.

Ramanujan grew up in southern India with little formal training in advanced maths. In 1913 he began sending Hardy pages of startling formulas, and Hardy arranged for him to come to England. He died in 1920, aged 32.

cards.title: Seven bridges, no route
cards.text: Königsberg had seven bridges linking two islands and the riverbanks. Could you walk across each exactly once? In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved you couldn't.
cards.source: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (presented 1736)
cards.more:
Euler threw away everything irrelevant, like the shapes of the land and the lengths of the bridges. All that mattered was which pieces of land connected to which. That turns the map into dots and lines, a graph, and it laid the foundations of graph theory.

Every time you pass through a piece of land you use two bridges, one in and one out. So apart from the start and finish, every piece needs an even number of bridges. In Königsberg all four had an odd number.

cards.title: The margin was too small
cards.text: Around 1637, Fermat wrote in a margin that aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no whole-number answers for n above 2. He claimed a proof the margin couldn't hold.
cards.source: Fermat's note in his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica (c. 1637); Wiles, Annals of Mathematics (1995)
cards.more:
It took 358 years. Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994, after about seven years of working largely in secret. The proof he announced in 1993 had a gap, and fixing it took another year, partly with help from his former student Richard Taylor. It was published in 1995.

Fermat almost certainly had no valid proof. Wiles used elliptic curves and modular forms, tools that didn't exist in Fermat's time.

cards.title: Add up 1 to 100, fast
cards.text: There's a trick that adds every whole number from 1 to 100 in seconds, in your head. What's the total, and what's the trick?
cards.source: Carl Friedrich Gauss, popular schoolroom story
cards.more:
5,050. Pair the numbers from the outside in: 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, and so on. There are 50 pairs, so the total is 50 × 101. In general, 1 to n adds up to n(n + 1)/2.

The trick is famously credited to a young Carl Friedrich Gauss, said to have stunned his teacher. The story comes from later retellings and grew along the way, so the details are legend. The method is real.

cards.title: Is 0.999... equal to 1?
cards.text: Write a decimal point followed by nines that go on forever. Is that number a tiny bit less than 1, or exactly 1?
cards.source: 0.999..., standard result in real analysis
cards.more:
Exactly 1. Quick argument: 1/3 = 0.333..., and three times that is 0.999..., but three times 1/3 is 1.

The discomfort comes from picturing the nines as a process that never finishes. In maths, 0.999... names the limit of 0.9, 0.99, 0.999 and so on, and that limit is 1. If it were less than 1 there'd be a gap, but after enough nines it's closer to 1 than any gap you can name.

cards.title: Fast thinking, slow thinking
cards.text: System 1 knows 2 + 2 instantly. System 2 grinds through 17 × 24. Most of the day, System 2 approves System 1's answers without checking.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman
cards.source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, part I (2011)
cards.more:
Daniel Kahneman says the two systems are characters in a story, not places in the brain. The labels came from psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West. Kahneman made them famous.

Fast thinking gets almost everything right, which is why we trust it when it's wrong. Its mistakes bunch up in predictable spots: numbers, probabilities, unfamiliar situations, and anything where a vivid story is easier than dull statistics. The next cards go through those spots.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: A spinning wheel moved their guesses
cards.text: After seeing a wheel stop on 10, people's average guess for the share of UN members that are African was 25%. After 65, it was 45%.
cards.source: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science (1974)
cards.more:
Psychologists call it anchoring. We start from whatever number is lying around and adjust too little. It replicated strongly in the Many Labs project in 2014, though studies using obviously random anchors, like a visible dice roll, found weaker effects.

Writing your own estimate down before you hear anyone else's blunts it. So does arguing for a number far from the anchor before settling. Anchors show up as the first price in a negotiation, or the 'was $200' on a sale tag.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: The letter K question
cards.text: People guess more English words start with K than have it third. Starting words are just easier to recall. K is third more often: ask, like, make, take.
cards.source: Tversky & Kahneman, Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability, Cognitive Psychology (1973)
cards.more:
The availability heuristic: we judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. Usually that works, because common things are easier to recall. But some things stick in memory for reasons that have nothing to do with how often they happen.

Plane crashes and shark attacks get heavy coverage, so they feel more common than quiet killers like heart disease. One recent bad experience with a supplier can outweigh years of good service in your head.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.text: The human understanding, when any proposition has been once laid down … forces everything else to add fresh support and confirmation...
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Novum Organum, book I, aphorism 46 (1620; ed. Joseph Devey)
cards.more:
Bacon described confirmation bias three centuries before psychologists named it. Once we hold a belief, we notice the evidence that fits and explain away the evidence that doesn't.

In the same aphorism he tells a story. A man is shown a temple's paintings of sailors who made vows to the gods and escaped shipwreck, and is pressed to admit the gods' power. He asks where the portraits are of those who made their vows and drowned anyway.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: The planes that never came back
cards.text: Abraham Wald studied damage on WWII bombers that made it home. The spots with few holes needed armour most. Planes hit there probably never came back.
cards.author: Abraham Wald
cards.source: Statistical Research Group memoranda on aircraft vulnerability, Columbia University (1943)
cards.more:
Survivorship bias means learning from the winners because the losers aren't around to be counted. Bacon's drowned sailors on the last card are the same idea.

It hides in everyday advice. Successful founders who dropped out of college tell you nothing until you count the dropouts who failed. Old buildings seem better made partly because the bad ones fell down. Wald's real memos were careful statistics on how vulnerable each part of a plane was, and the popular story simplifies them.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: Everyone is biased except me
cards.text: In a survey of over 600 Americans, more than 85% said they were less biased than the average American. Exactly one said they were more biased.
cards.em: less biased than the average American
cards.source: Scopelliti et al., Management Science (2015); term coined by Pronin, Lin & Ross (2002)
cards.more:
The name for this is the bias blind spot. Emily Pronin's explanation is the introspection illusion. We judge other people by what they do. We judge ourselves by looking inward, finding no biased motives and deciding we're fair. But bias doesn't show up when you look inward. It works below that.

So reading about biases mostly makes people better at diagnosing their friends. Pronin, Lin and Ross coined the term in 2002.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.title: Pretend the plan already failed
cards.text: Before a big decision, assume it's a year later and the plan has failed. Everyone writes down why. This is Gary Klein's premortem.
cards.author: Gary Klein
cards.source: Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review (2007)
cards.more:
Klein argues it surfaces risks people were too polite or too confident to raise. Doubt becomes an assignment instead of an insult.

It fits this thread. You can't feel your own biases working, so the checks have to live in the routine. Others with decent support: write your estimate before hearing anyone else's, and keep a decision journal. In experiments by Lord, Lepper and Preston, just asking people to consider the opposite reduced biased reading of evidence.

thread.title: Your brain's shortcuts in 7 cards

cards.text: Millions of items … are present to my senses which never properly enter into my experience. … My experience is what I agree to attend to.
cards.em: what I agree to attend to
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. 11 'Attention' (1890)
cards.more:
William James wrote this in 1890. His point is that the world doesn't just pour in. At every moment you pick a sliver of what's there, and those picks, repeated day after day, become the texture of your life.

Today a lot of companies compete to do the picking for you. Feeds and notifications are both bids for the 'agree' part of his sentence.

cards.text: Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits … We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone.
cards.author: William James
cards.source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 1, ch. 4 'Habit' (1890)
cards.more:
James's chapter on habit holds up well. He argued habits are physical: repeated actions wear paths into the nervous system, and each path makes the next repetition easier.

His advice was concrete. Start a new habit as strongly and decidedly as you can. Allow no exceptions until it's rooted, because one lapse undoes more than one success builds. And act on a good resolution at the first chance, instead of just enjoying the feeling of having made it.

cards.text: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
cards.em: stay quietly in their own chamber
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, no. 139 (1670; trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Pascal meant diversion: chasing games, gossip, work and ventures mostly to avoid being alone with our own thoughts.

A 2014 study led by Timothy Wilson made it vivid. Many people left alone in a bare room for 6 to 15 minutes, with nothing to do but think, chose to give themselves a mild electric shock, even though they'd said earlier they would pay to avoid one. Men did it far more often than women.

cards.title: Only a third replicated
cards.text: 270 researchers redid 100 published psychology studies in 2015. Of 97 originally significant results, only 36% were significant again. Effects averaged about half the original size.
cards.source: Open Science Collaboration, Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science, Science (2015)
cards.more:
It became a landmark of what's now called the replication crisis. It doesn't mean two-thirds of psychology is false. A failed replication can come from a weak original, a weak redo, or real differences between the two. But one published result, especially a small surprising one, is weaker evidence than it looks.

The field changed habits after this: registering hypotheses before collecting data, bigger samples, and many-lab replications of famous effects.

cards.title: Willpower tanks and power poses
cards.text: Ego depletion said willpower runs out like fuel. Power posing said a superhero stance changes your hormones and boldness. In big careful replications, both main effects largely vanished.
cards.source: Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science (2016); Dana Carney's public statement (2016)
cards.more:
The ego depletion replication ran in 23 labs with a pre-registered protocol and found an effect close to zero. A later 36-lab project with over 3,500 people found the same. For power posing, a larger 2015 study found no hormone changes, and in 2016 co-author Dana Carney wrote that she no longer believed the effect was real.

Amy Cuddy still argues posture can change people's feelings of power, a much smaller claim.

cards.title: They chose the longer pain
cards.text: One trial: 60 seconds of painfully cold water. The other: the same, plus 30 seconds while it warmed one degree. Most people chose to repeat the longer one.
cards.em: chose to repeat the longer one
cards.source: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, Psychological Science (1993)
cards.more:
This is the peak-end rule. Memory roughly averages the worst moment and the last moment, and mostly ignores how long the thing lasted. Kahneman calls that second blind spot duration neglect.

Later work with colonoscopy patients found the same pattern. Ending the procedure more gently made people remember it as less unpleasant, even though it lasted longer.

cards.title: Are the clueless the most confident?
cards.text: Dunning-Kruger is usually summed up as: the less people know, the more they think they're geniuses. Is that what the 1999 research found?
cards.source: Kruger & Dunning, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1999)
cards.more:
Not quite. In the 1999 studies, people in the bottom quarter on tests of logic, grammar and humour put themselves around the 62nd percentile on average. They were really near the 12th. A big overestimate, but they rated themselves only somewhat above average, not top.

There's also a live debate about how much is a statistical artefact. Almost everyone rates themselves a bit above average, and regression to the mean alone can produce a similar-looking chart.

cards.title: Does a marshmallow predict your future?
cards.text: Kids who waited longer for a second marshmallow in the Stanford experiments did better years later. Does a four-year-old's self-control set the course of their life?
cards.em: set the course of their life
cards.source: Watts, Duncan & Quan, Psychological Science (2018)
cards.more:
Much less than the story suggests. The original follow-ups were small. In 2018 Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan ran a conceptual replication with a sample over ten times larger and far more diverse. The link to later achievement was about half the original size, and shrank further after accounting for family background and early cognitive ability.

Other work found children wait longer when the adult has proved trustworthy.

cards.title: Left-brained or right-brained?
cards.text: Personality quizzes love to say logical people are left-brained and creative people are right-brained. Is there anything to it?
cards.source: Nielsen et al., PLOS ONE (2013)
cards.more:
Not as a personality type. Some functions are lopsided. For most people, key language areas sit in the left hemisphere, and the split-brain studies of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga in the 1960s showed the two halves handle information differently.

But a 2013 University of Utah study looked at brain scans from more than 1,000 people and found no sign that individuals are left-dominant or right-dominant overall. Creativity and logic both use networks spread across both sides.

cards.title: Stressed, or dreading Tuesday?
cards.text: Some people just feel bad. Others can tell irritated from disappointed from anxious. Lisa Feldman Barrett calls this emotional granularity, and sharper labels seem to help people cope.
cards.author: Lisa Feldman Barrett
cards.source: How Emotions Are Made (2017)
cards.more:
Barrett noticed it in the 1990s. Some study participants used anxious, sad and angry almost interchangeably, while others drew sharp lines between them. Later research links higher granularity with more flexible emotion regulation, and lower granularity with depression and anxiety, though cause and effect are hard to untangle.

A specific feeling points to a specific response. 'Stressed' doesn't say much. 'Behind on work' or 'embarrassed about that email' each suggest a different next step.

cards.title: Losses hit about twice as hard
cards.text: People often refuse a coin flip where heads wins $150 and tails loses $100. It's a good bet. Losing $100 hurts more than winning $100 feels good.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
cards.source: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk, Econometrica (1979)
cards.more:
Kahneman and Tversky found that in typical studies, losses weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains. That helps explain why people hold losing investments too long, and why 'don't lose your discount' can beat 'get a discount'.

It isn't a universal law. Later research found it weaker or absent for small stakes, and some researchers say effects blamed on it, like sticking with the status quo, are better explained by plain inertia. The figure of two is an average.

cards.title: The box that's already ticked
cards.text: Where you must opt in to be an organ donor, registered consent tends to be low. In similar opt-out countries, it's near universal. Only the default changed.
cards.author: Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein
cards.source: Do Defaults Save Lives?, Science (2003)
cards.more:
Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein made this famous in Science in 2003. Defaults work for several reasons: switching takes effort, the default feels like a recommendation, and staying put feels safer. Thaler and Sunstein built much of Nudge around this, and automatic enrolment in workplace pensions is one of its biggest successes.

One caveat. Actual donation rates differ far less than registration rates, because families, hospitals and infrastructure matter a lot.

cards.title: They're careless, I'm just busy
cards.text: Someone cuts you off: selfish driver. You cut someone off: you were late. Lee Ross named the first half the fundamental attribution error.
cards.author: Lee Ross
cards.source: The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (1977)
cards.more:
It means explaining other people's actions by their character and underrating their circumstances. The classic demonstration came in 1967. Edward Jones and Victor Harris had people read essays praising or attacking Fidel Castro. Even when told the writers had been assigned a side, readers still judged them to believe what they'd argued.

The effect is real but varies. It seems weaker in cultures that pay more attention to context, and later reviews found the self-versus-others version less consistent than once thought.

cards.title: Nerves or readiness?
cards.text: James Gross compared two ways of handling emotion. Suppression hides it. Reappraisal reads the situation differently, like treating pre-talk nerves as readiness. Reappraisal tends to work better.
cards.author: James Gross
cards.source: Gross & John, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2003)
cards.more:
Gross sorts emotion regulation by timing. Reappraisal acts early, changing what a situation means before the feeling fully builds. Suppression acts late, clamping down on a feeling that's already running.

In lab studies, suppressing didn't make people feel less bad. It raised physiological arousal and hurt memory for what was happening. In daily life, people who habitually reappraise tend to report more positive emotion and closer relationships than habitual suppressors.

cards.text: The butcher has more meat in his shop than he himself can consume … But they have nothing to offer in exchange…
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 4, Of the Origin and Use of Money (1776)
cards.more:
This is the textbook story of where money came from. The brewer and the baker want the butcher's meat, but he already has all the bread and beer he needs, so no trade happens. Economists later called it the double coincidence of wants.

Smith's fix is that people started keeping something everyone would accept, like cattle, salt, shells or metal, and that became money. The story has shaped economics for 250 years. The next card asks whether it ever happened.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Debt came before money
