cards.text: Nobody has found a society that ran on everyday barter, David Graeber noted. Neighbours tracked who owed whom. In his account, debt came first, coins later.
cards.author: David Graeber
cards.source: Debt: The First 5,000 Years (2011)
cards.more:
Graeber was an anthropologist, and others in his field had reported this long before him. Barter, where it exists, tends to happen between strangers who don't trust each other, rarely between neighbours who see each other daily.

In a village, if you need the butcher's meat now, you take it and owe him. The debt gets remembered and settled later, often in some other form. Some of the oldest writing from Mesopotamia, thousands of years before coins, is records of what people owed.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: The shekel was a weight first
cards.text: The shekel started as a unit of weight in Mesopotamia, attested by about 2150 BC. Hammurabi's code priced a year of unskilled labour in shekels of silver.
cards.em: started as a unit of weight
cards.source: Wikipedia, Shekel
cards.more:
The name comes from a Semitic root meaning to weigh, and a shekel was simply a set amount of silver on a scale. The Code of Hammurabi dates to around 1750 BC.

Much everyday dealing involved no silver changing hands. Temple and palace administrators recorded debts in shekels, and people settled them in barley or other goods at an agreed rate. Money was a unit of account long before anyone stamped a coin.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: The first coins came from Lydia
cards.text: The oldest known coins come from Lydia, in today's western Turkey, around the 7th century BC. Their stamp promised a standard weight, so nobody had to weigh them.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Lydia
cards.more:
They were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver that washed down Lydia's rivers. Herodotus wrote that the Lydians were the first people known to strike coins of gold and silver.

Their most famous king, Croesus, whose name still means fabulously rich, is credited with the first coins of pure gold and pure silver. Coins spread fast through the Greek world. You could trust one without a scale, as long as you trusted whoever stamped it.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Iron coins gave us paper money
cards.text: The first paper money appeared in Sichuan, China, in the 11th century. Iron coins there were heavy and worth little, so merchants issued notes called jiaozi.
cards.em: first paper money appeared in Sichuan
cards.source: Wikipedia, Jiaozi (currency)
cards.more:
The early notes worked like receipts. You deposited iron cash, carried the slip and redeemed it later, which beat hauling strings of coins through mountains and rivers. Merchant groups soon standardized them, and the Song government took over.

State notes were printed in several colours with seals against counterfeiting. The paper itself was worthless, so its value rested on trust in the issuer and on not printing too much. Later Chinese governments learned that the hard way.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Bad money drives out good
cards.text: If a full silver coin and a debased one must legally be worth the same, people hoard the good one and spend the bad. That's Gresham's law.
cards.author: Thomas Gresham
cards.source: Gresham's law, named by Henry Dunning Macleod in 1857 after Sir Thomas Gresham (1519-1579)
cards.more:
Thomas Gresham was a Tudor financier who advised Elizabeth I after her father, Henry VIII, had badly debased England's coins. He didn't discover the idea. Nicole Oresme and Copernicus described it, and Aristophanes joked about it in ancient Athens. Henry Dunning Macleod named it after Gresham in 1857.

Debasement tempts rulers because shaving metal from each coin lets a government spend more without raising taxes. The cost lands quietly on everyone holding money.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.text: There is no subtler, no surer means of overturning the existing basis of society than to debauch the currency.
cards.author: John Maynard Keynes
cards.source: The Economic Consequences of the Peace, ch. 6 (1919)
cards.more:
Keynes wrote this in 1919, after resigning from the British delegation at the Paris peace talks in protest at the reparations imposed on Germany. A few lines earlier he notes that Lenin is said to have called this the best way to destroy capitalism.

His point is that inflation is a hidden tax. Governments can quietly confiscate a large part of their citizens' wealth, enriching some and ruining others, while everyone blames speculators. Within four years Germany was in hyperinflation.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.title: Money runs on mutual trust
cards.text: A banknote is just paper, yet total strangers accept it. Yuval Noah Harari calls money the most universal and efficient system of mutual trust ever invented.
cards.em: system of mutual trust ever invented
cards.author: Yuval Noah Harari
cards.source: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, ch. 10 (English edition, 2014)
cards.more:
It works between people who share nothing else, not even a language or a religion. Most money today isn't even paper. It's entries in bank databases.

This thread followed that trust. Smith imagined a handy commodity, Graeber put debt first, Mesopotamian scribes kept score in silver, Lydian kings stamped metal and Song China made it paper. For Harari, shared stories like money are what let millions of strangers cooperate.

thread.title: Where money came from (8 cards)

cards.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
cards.em: their regard to their own interest
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 2 (1776)
cards.more:
This may be the most quoted line in economics, and it often gets misread as greed is good. Smith meant something narrower. Trade lets strangers serve each other without being friends. The baker doesn't have to love you, he just has to want your money.

Smith also wrote a whole book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, on sympathy and conscience. He didn't think people were only selfish. He thought markets work even when they are.

cards.text: People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public…
cards.author: Adam Smith
cards.source: The Wealth of Nations, Book 1, ch. 10 (1776)
cards.more:
The sentence ends: or in some contrivance to raise prices. People who see Smith as a cheerleader for business are often surprised. He distrusted merchants and manufacturers whenever they could escape competition, and watched them lobby for monopolies and tariffs at the public's expense.

In the next sentence he admits such meetings can't be banned without trampling liberty. He argued the law shouldn't make them easier, for example by making traders register together.

cards.text: …the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it…
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 1, Economy (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau applies it to houses right away. An average house near Concord cost about eight hundred dollars, and saving that would take a labourer ten to fifteen years of his life.

The same sum works on anything. Divide a price by what you earn per hour after tax, and you get the hours of life it costs. Thoreau tracked every expense of his Walden cabin down to the half cent, to see how little he needed.

cards.text: …they go mad in herds, while they only recover their senses slowly, and one by one.
cards.author: Charles Mackay
cards.source: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds, Preface (1841)
cards.more:
Mackay's book covers the Mississippi Company scheme in France and the South Sea Bubble in Britain, which both collapsed in 1720, plus the Dutch tulip craze of the 1630s.

He exaggerated some of it. Historian Anne Goldgar's research suggests tulip mania was much smaller than his account, with few documented ruinations, and he leaned on moralizing pamphlets. His main point has held up through railway shares, dot-com stocks and crypto.

cards.title: Wealth is what you don't see
cards.text: Spending is visible and wealth isn't, says Morgan Housel. All you know about someone in an expensive car is that they now have less money.
cards.em: Spending is visible and wealth isn't
cards.author: Morgan Housel
cards.source: The Psychology of Money, ch. 9 (2020)
cards.more:
Real wealth, in his telling, is the cars not bought and the money not spent, sitting where nobody can see it. Since we learn what rich looks like by watching what rich people buy, we copy the spending and miss the saving.

He calls a related idea the man in the car paradox. People who see a flashy car rarely think about the driver. They picture themselves in it. Housel sees wealth as choices for later, rather than status now.

cards.title: Skin in the game
cards.text: Nassim Taleb distrusts anyone who gets the upside of a decision while someone else bears the downside. Bankers whose risks blow up on taxpayers, for example.
cards.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
cards.source: Skin in the Game (2018)
cards.more:
Pundits who never pay for bad forecasts fit too. Taleb points to the Code of Hammurabi, almost 4,000 years old. If a house collapsed and killed its owner, the builder was put to death, so the person who knew the risk also carried it.

For Taleb this is about feedback more than punishment. People who pay for their mistakes learn or leave the field. People who don't keep making them. His test for advice is what the adviser loses if wrong.

cards.title: When a number becomes a goal
cards.text: Economist Charles Goodhart noticed that a statistic used to steer policy stops behaving once people manage toward it. They hit the number without delivering what it measured.
cards.author: Charles Goodhart
cards.source: Problems of Monetary Management: The UK Experience (1975)
cards.more:
Goodhart, at the Bank of England, was writing about money supply figures. When the government targeted one measure of money, the financial system changed its behaviour, and the measure stopped tracking what policymakers cared about.

The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later gave it the snappy general form people quote now. It shows up in hospitals measured on waiting times, schools judged on test scores and programmers paid by lines of code.

cards.title: The coin flip people refuse
cards.text: Offered a coin flip that wins 150 dollars or loses 100, most people say no, even though the odds favour them. Losses loom larger than gains.
cards.author: Daniel Kahneman
cards.source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, part 4 (2011); Kahneman and Tversky, Prospect Theory (1979)
cards.more:
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky measured this. Losses feel roughly one and a half to two and a half times as strong as equal gains. Loss aversion was a core part of their prospect theory, published in 1979, which later earned Kahneman the Nobel prize in economics. Tversky died before it was awarded.

It shows up in daily life. Investors hold losing stocks to avoid making the loss real, and shoppers react more to dodging a fee than to the same discount.

cards.title: Portugal, England, wine and cloth
cards.text: David Ricardo showed two countries both gain from trade even when one is better at making everything. Each sticks to what it gives up least to make.
cards.author: David Ricardo
cards.source: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ch. 7 (1817)
cards.more:
In Ricardo's numbers, Portugal needs 80 workers a year for a batch of wine and 90 for cloth. England needs 120 for wine and 100 for cloth. Portugal is better at both but much better at wine, so it makes wine and buys cloth, England does the reverse, and both end up with more.

It's called comparative advantage, and it works for people too. A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by handing over the typing.

cards.title: The great Hanoi rat bounty
cards.text: In 1902 colonial Hanoi paid one cent per rat tail. Soon officials spotted live rats without tails. People cut off tails and freed the rats to breed.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Hanoi Rat Massacre (citing historian Michael Vann)
cards.more:
The French colonial government feared plague, and hundreds of thousands of rats were killed. But it paid for a proxy, tails, instead of what it wanted, fewer rats. A tailless rat that keeps breeding makes more tails, and there were reports of rat farming too. The bounty was cancelled.

A similar cobra bounty story from British India gets told a lot, but the Hanoi case is the one historian Michael Vann documented in colonial archives.

cards.title: Mansa Musa's gold in Cairo
cards.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa of Mali gave away so much gold in Cairo, on his way to Mecca, that its value there dropped, says the historian al-Umari.
cards.source: Al-Umari, as cited in Wikipedia, Mansa Musa
cards.more:
Al-Umari says a measure of gold worth 25 silver dirhams fell below 22 and stayed there for at least twelve years. Mali controlled some of the richest gold sources of the medieval world, and the trip put it on European maps.

Online the story gets inflated into Musa wrecking Egypt's economy. The historian Warren Schultz argues the drop was within normal price swings of the period. Musa also ran short on the way home and borrowed from Cairo merchants.

cards.title: The bat and the ball
cards.text: A bat and a ball cost 1.10 dollars in total. The bat costs 1.00 dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
cards.em: How much does the ball cost?
cards.source: Shane Frederick, Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2005)
cards.more:
Five cents. Ten cents jumps to mind, but then the bat would be 1.10 and the total 1.20. A 5 cent ball and a 1.05 dollar bat add up to 1.10, exactly a dollar apart.

The puzzle is from Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test, and Daniel Kahneman made it famous in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Plenty of students at top universities miss it. The math is easy. A quick, confident answer shows up first, and nobody checks it.

cards.title: Grains on a chessboard
cards.text: One grain of wheat on the first square of a chessboard, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. Roughly how many grains in total?
cards.source: Wikipedia, Wheat and chessboard problem
cards.more:
About 18.4 quintillion, or 2 to the power of 64 minus one. That's 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, far more wheat than humanity has ever grown.

In the legend, the inventor of chess asks a king for this reward, and the king laughs at how modest it sounds. The first 32 squares hold only about four billion grains in total. The second half is where it explodes. Compound growth in savings or debt has the same shape.

cards.title: Darwin's three-ingredient recipe
cards.text: Darwin's argument needs three things. Individuals vary. Much of that variation is inherited. Far more are born than survive. So helpful traits spread. That's natural selection.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 4 (1859)
cards.more:
None of the three was controversial on its own. Breeders knew animals vary and pass traits on, and Thomas Malthus had written about populations outgrowing their food. Darwin, and independently Alfred Russel Wallace, saw what happens when all three act over immense spans of time. Their ideas were first presented together in 1858.

No goal or designer is needed. Selection filters each generation, keeping what works a bit better there and then. This thread goes step by step.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: …the slowest breeder of all known animals … at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 3 (1859)
cards.more:
This is the pressure behind natural selection. Every species can multiply faster than its world can support. Darwin chose the elephant on purpose, the slowest breeder he knew. In later editions he redid the sums and got nearly nineteen million elephants after about 750 years.

Elephant numbers don't actually explode, so most young of every species must die before breeding. Darwin called this the struggle for existence. Any small inherited edge changes who gets to be a parent.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Soot turned the moths black
cards.text: Peppered moths are usually pale, blending into lichen-covered bark. Then Industrial Revolution soot blackened England's trees. By 1895, 98 percent of moths recorded near Manchester were dark.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Peppered moth evolution
cards.more:
Birds hunt moths by sight. On pale bark, dark moths got eaten. On sooty bark, pale ones did. After clean-air laws took effect, the pale form came back. That's natural selection, visible within a human lifetime.

Bernard Kettlewell studied this between 1953 and 1956, and his work was later attacked, even accused of fraud. The geneticist Michael Majerus then ran a careful seven-year study starting in 2001, published after his death in 2012. It backed Kettlewell in detail.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Darwin's finches, caught evolving
cards.text: On the Galápagos island of Daphne Major, a 1977 drought left mostly big, tough seeds. Many finches died. The next generation had measurably larger beaks.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Peter and Rosemary Grant; Darwin's finches
cards.more:
Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied the finches there since 1973, catching, measuring and blood-sampling them for six months of every year. Darwin assumed selection was too slow to watch. In the 1977 rainy season only 24 millimetres of rain fell, so small soft seeds ran out and birds that could crack hard ones survived.

It can run the other way too. After a 2003 drought, with a bigger rival finch species on the island, the medium ground finch's average beak got smaller.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: Whales once walked on land
cards.text: About 50 million years ago, in what is now South Asia, wolf-like animals such as Pakicetus lived around water. Their descendants became whales. Whales' closest living relatives are hippos.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Evolution of cetaceans; Pakicetus
cards.more:
Whale evolution is one of the best-documented changes in the fossil record. It runs from Pakicetus at the water's edge, through Ambulocetus, whose name means walking whale, to fully marine forms with shrunken hind limbs.

Many living whales still carry small pelvic bones deep inside the body. Gene studies, independent of the fossils, put whales among the even-toed hoofed mammals, sharing an ancestor with hippos around 55 million years ago.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.title: One code for all life
cards.text: Bacteria, mushrooms, oak trees and you read DNA with nearly the same code: 64 three-letter codons. So engineered bacteria have made human insulin for medicine since 1982.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Genetic code; Insulin (medication)
cards.more:
Nothing forced the code to be this way. Francis Crick suggested it may be a frozen accident, fixed early and then locked in, because changing it would scramble almost every protein a cell makes. That nearly all life shares it is strong evidence of one common ancestor.

Biologists call that ancestor LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. Most studies put it at least 3.5 billion years ago. The finches on Daphne Major and the bacteria in your gut are distant cousins through it.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: There is grandeur in this view of life … from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 14 (1859)
cards.more:
These are the last words of the first edition of the Origin. Look at the end: have been, and are being, evolved. Darwin knew evolution was still happening, as the moths and finches in this thread show.

The thread in one breath: living things vary, much of that is inherited, far more are born than survive, and so the environment keeps editing every species. Given time, that links whales to hippos and you to everything alive.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

cards.text: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.
cards.author: John Muir
cards.source: My First Summer in the Sierra, ch. 6 (1911)
cards.more:
In 1869 a young John Muir spent a summer in California's Sierra Nevada, working with a flock of sheep being driven to mountain pastures. His journal from those months became this book in 1911.

The line usually gets passed around in looser paraphrases. This is how he actually wrote it, and it's the heart of what we now call ecology. Muir went on to co-found the Sierra Club.

cards.text: Hence, both in space and time, we seem to be brought somewhat near to that great fact—that mystery of mysteries—the first appearance of new beings on this earth.
cards.author: Charles Darwin
cards.source: The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 17 (2nd ed., 1845)
cards.more:
Darwin wrote this about the Galápagos Islands, which HMS Beagle reached in September 1835. Such young volcanic islands, with lava flows still sharp, held many creatures found nowhere else.

The phrase was borrowed. The astronomer John Herschel used it in an 1836 letter to the geologist Charles Lyell, about how extinct species get replaced by new ones. On the Origin of Species, published 24 years after the visit, was Darwin's answer.

cards.text: Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 16, The Pond in Winter (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau wrote this after cutting through a foot of snow and a foot of ice on Walden Pond. Kneeling to drink, he looked down into what he called the quiet parlor of the fishes, lit softly as if through ground glass.

In the same chapter, people claimed the pond was bottomless. So he sounded it with a cod-line and a stone. Its greatest depth was exactly one hundred and two feet.

cards.title: Water bears in open space
cards.text: Dried-out tardigrades spent 10 days riding outside a spacecraft in 2007, exposed to the vacuum of space. Rehydrated back on Earth, they revived and went on laying eggs.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Tardigrade (FOTON-M3 mission)
cards.more:
Tardigrades, or water bears, are tiny eight-legged animals. When the moss or pond they live in dries out, they pull in their legs, lose almost all their water and their metabolism stops. In this state, called a tun, they can wait out conditions that kill nearly anything else.

Vacuum alone had no significant effect on them. Unfiltered solar ultraviolet light killed most, though a few still recovered. On mosses they can reach over 2 million per square metre.

cards.title: A shark born before Darwin
cards.text: Greenland sharks may be the longest-lived vertebrates. Dating their eye lenses suggests at least 272 years. The oldest studied was put at 392 years, give or take 120.
cards.source: Nielsen et al., Science (2016); Wikipedia: Greenland shark
cards.more:
Sharks have no bony parts that lay down yearly rings, so their age was a mystery. In 2016 researchers dated the core of the eye lens, which forms during development and never changes. Its carbon-14, including the spike from bomb tests in the 1950s and 60s, gave each shark's birth date.

They live in the cold North Atlantic and Arctic, grow over 6 metres long and don't mature until around 150. Some alive today were born before Charles Darwin.

cards.title: 2.4 million new cells a second
cards.text: An adult makes about 2.4 million new red blood cells every second. Each lasts roughly 100 to 120 days. At any moment you carry some 20 to 30 trillion.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Red blood cell
cards.more:
They're by far the most numerous cells in your body. As they mature in the bone marrow, they lose their nucleus and most of their machinery to make room for haemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that carries oxygen. With no nucleus they can't divide or repair themselves, so they need constant replacing.

A typical one makes a full lap of your body in about a minute. Over three to four months, that's well over a hundred thousand trips.

cards.title: The ten-to-one bacteria myth
cards.text: A popular claim says your bacteria outnumber your cells ten to one. A 2016 recount found about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells.
cards.source: Sender, Fuchs and Milo, PLoS Biology and Cell (2016); Wikipedia: Human microbiome
cards.more:
That's for a typical adult man. The ten-to-one figure came from rough estimates in the 1970s that got repeated for decades without being checked. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo at the Weizmann Institute redid the sums with modern data. Blood cells make up about 90 percent of the human count.

By weight your bacteria come to about 0.2 kilograms. Most live in your gut, where they help digest food and train your immune system.

cards.title: A tree older than the pyramids
cards.text: Methuselah, a Great Basin bristlecone pine, started growing around 2833 BC. It was already centuries old when the Great Pyramid of Giza was finished.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Pinus longaeva
cards.more:
That makes it more than 4,850 years old, credited as the oldest known living non-clonal organism. Bristlecones grow very slowly, high in the cold, dry mountains of the western United States. As an old tree ages, much of it can die back until a narrow strip of bark links the roots to a few living branches.

Some clonal colonies, like aspen groves sharing one root system, may be older. Methuselah is a single tree.

cards.title: Bees give directions by dancing
cards.text: A honeybee back from good flowers does a waggle dance. Its angle from straight up gives the food's direction from the Sun. How long she waggles gives the distance.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Waggle dance; Karl von Frisch
cards.more:
Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, was one of the first to decode this, through years of experiments with marked bees and feeding stations. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Inside the dark hive the comb hangs vertically, so straight up stands in for the Sun. A run straight up means fly toward the Sun. A run angled right means fly that angle to the right of it. Other bees follow the dancer, then head out.

cards.title: Your cells hold ancient bacteria
cards.text: Lynn Margulis pushed a once-doubted idea: mitochondria, the power units in your cells, were once free-living bacteria. One cell swallowed another and, instead of digesting it, kept it.
cards.author: Lynn Margulis
cards.source: On the Origin of Mitosing Cells, Journal of Theoretical Biology (1967)
cards.more:
Plant chloroplasts started the same way. The idea, called endosymbiotic theory, was proposed in 1905 and 1910 by the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski but largely ignored. Margulis revived it in 1967 with microbiological evidence.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small chromosomes, separate from the cell's main DNA, and split in two the way bacteria do. Chloroplasts even share a double membrane with free-living cyanobacteria. It's now standard textbook biology.

cards.title: Evolution from the gene's view
cards.text: Richard Dawkins suggested looking at evolution from the gene's side. Bodies die, genes get copied. Genes that build bodies good at surviving and breeding get copied more.
cards.author: Richard Dawkins
cards.source: The Selfish Gene (1976)
cards.more:
In The Selfish Gene he called organisms vehicles that genes build to get themselves passed on. The word selfish trips people up. Dawkins meant only that the genes around today are the ones that were good at getting copied, with no desires involved.

This helps explain why animals help relatives, who likely carry copies of the same genes. That idea, kin selection, came largely from W. D. Hamilton's work. The book also introduced the word meme.

cards.title: Are you still the same body?
cards.text: Red blood cells last about four months. About a tenth of your fat cells are renewed each year. If enough gets swapped out, are you still you?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Ship of Theseus; Bomb pulse
cards.more:
Only partly, because you aren't replaced evenly. The old puzzle is the Ship of Theseus, rebuilt plank by plank. The idea that your whole body renews every seven years is too simple.

In 2005 Kirsty Spalding and colleagues used carbon-14 from Cold War nuclear tests, locked into DNA as cells formed, to date human cells. Many tissues turn over, but neurons in your cerebral cortex basically don't. They're about as old as you are.

cards.title: Which came first, chicken or egg?
cards.text: Philosophers argued over it for centuries, but evolution gives a clear answer. Before you tap for more: did the first chicken hatch from an egg, or lay one?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Chicken or the egg
cards.more:
The egg, by a long way. Hard-shelled eggs that could be laid on dry land appeared around 312 million years ago, long before any bird existed. Fish and amphibians laid eggs earlier still.

Even counting only chicken eggs, the egg wins. Species change gradually, so at some point two birds that were almost chickens produced an egg holding a bird we'd call a chicken. Its chicken DNA was already in the egg before it hatched.

cards.title: Why choice makes us dizzy
cards.text: Kierkegaard compared anxiety to standing at a cliff edge. The dizziness is partly knowing you could jump. For him, anxiety is what freedom feels like from the inside.
cards.author: Søren Kierkegaard
cards.source: The Concept of Anxiety (1844)
cards.more:
Søren Kierkegaard, a 19th-century Danish thinker often called the first existentialist, published much of his work under made-up names. In The Concept of Anxiety (1844) he separates fear, which has an object, from anxiety, which is about possibility itself. On a height you feel dizzy partly because nothing is stopping you.

The thinkers in this thread all start from the same place. Being human means facing choices no rulebook can settle for you.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.text: If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.
cards.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
cards.source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Missiles 12 (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911)
cards.more:
Nietzsche wrote this in 1888, in a run of short, punchy aphorisms. It got famous in the 20th century when the psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, a Holocaust survivor, quoted a version of it in Man’s Search for Meaning to explain how some prisoners found the strength to endure.

Nietzsche matters to existentialism because he argued the old sources of meaning were fading, and people would have to make their own values. A ‘wherefore’ gives freedom a direction.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: Nobody is born a coward
cards.text: A paper knife is designed before it’s made. Sartre said people are the reverse: we exist first, with no built-in purpose, then define ourselves by what we do.
cards.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
cards.source: Existentialism Is a Humanism (lecture 1945, published 1946)
cards.more:
Jean-Paul Sartre gave this lecture in Paris in 1945, and it became the best-known summary of existentialism. His slogan was ‘existence precedes essence’. With no creator designing human nature in advance, there’s no blueprint to check. Nobody is born a coward or a hero.

So ‘that’s just how I am’ never fully works as an excuse. Sartre added that choosing for yourself also sketches what you think a person should be.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: The waiter who plays a waiter
cards.text: Sartre describes a café waiter who moves a little too precisely, as if acting the part. That’s bad faith, hiding from your freedom behind a role.
cards.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
cards.source: Being and Nothingness (1943)
cards.more:
If we make ourselves, why do so few people feel free? Sartre’s answer was bad faith, a self-deception where we hide from our own freedom. The waiter treats ‘waiter’ as his whole essence. The rest of us say ‘I’m just not a creative person’ or ‘my job made me do it’.

Sartre wasn’t mocking waiters, or roles in general. His target was pretending the role does the choosing for you. Bad faith’s favourite line is ‘I had no choice’.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: My freedom needs yours
cards.text: Simone de Beauvoir argued that if freedom gives life its value, you can’t want it only for yourself. To will yourself free is also to will others free.
cards.author: Simone de Beauvoir
cards.source: The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947)
cards.more:
Beauvoir wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) partly to answer a common attack: if there are no fixed values, isn’t everything permitted? She said no. We’re ambiguous creatures, free but tied to bodies, history and other people, and real freedom only grows where others are free too.

Two years later The Second Sex applied this to women, showing how society had cast them as a fixed ‘other’ instead of free subjects.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: Sisyphus, smiling
cards.text: The gods sentenced Sisyphus to roll a boulder uphill forever. It always rolls back. Camus saw us in him, then asked us to picture Sisyphus happy.
cards.author: Albert Camus
cards.source: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942)
cards.more:
Camus called the clash between our hunger for meaning and the world’s silence ‘the absurd’. He asked whether it makes life not worth living, and answered no. You live with it, eyes open. He called that response revolt.

Sisyphus is his hero because he knows exactly how hopeless his task is and keeps pushing, owning every step. Camus rejected the existentialist label. Where Sartre says we create meaning, Camus says we can live fully even without it.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.title: Choices you pretend aren’t choices
cards.text: Name one thing in your life you call ‘just how it is’. What if it’s a choice you keep making every day?
cards.source: Drawing on Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943), and Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942)
cards.more:
The thinkers in this thread would say it often is, at least in part. Kierkegaard said freedom makes us dizzy. Nietzsche said we need a why. Sartre said there’s no fixed human nature and we hide from that in bad faith. Beauvoir said real freedom includes other people’s. Camus said we can live fully without answers from the universe.

None of them claimed every circumstance is chosen. Illness, poverty and other people’s actions are real limits.

thread.title: Existentialism in 7 cards

cards.text: …daily to discourse about virtue … is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living…
cards.author: Socrates (as written by Plato)
cards.source: Apology, 38a (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871)
cards.more:
Socrates said this at his trial in Athens in 399 BC, after the jury found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. Instead of begging for mercy, he explained that he couldn’t stop questioning people.

‘Examined’ here means tested in conversation. What do you believe about justice or courage, and does it hold up when someone pushes? The jury sentenced him to death.

cards.text: …men come to be builders, for instance, by building … by doing just actions we come to be just … and by doing brave actions brave.
cards.author: Aristotle
cards.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book 2.1 (trans. D. P. Chase)
cards.more:
Aristotle treats character like a craft. Nobody becomes a harpist by reading about harps, and nobody becomes brave by admiring bravery. You become what you do over and over.

That was a quietly radical idea. It makes virtue a skill rather than a gift you either have or lack. It starts clumsy and turns into second nature with practice.

cards.text: …all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
cards.em: stay quietly in their own chamber
cards.author: Blaise Pascal
cards.source: Pensées, 139 (trans. W. F. Trotter)
cards.more:
Blaise Pascal was a mathematician and inventor who, late in life, gathered notes for a defence of Christianity. He died in 1662 before finishing it, and the fragments came out as the Pensées, or ‘thoughts’. This one is from a section on diversion.

Pascal saw people chase games, wars and busyness mostly to avoid sitting alone with their thoughts. In a 2014 study, many participants chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than sit alone with nothing to do for a few minutes.

cards.text: When I play with my cat who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me?
cards.em: more sport than she makes me
cards.author: Michel de Montaigne
cards.source: Essays, Book 2.12, Apology for Raimond Sebond (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt)
cards.more:
Michel de Montaigne more or less invented the essay, a word that means ‘attempt’ in French. This line sits inside his longest one, where he pokes holes in human arrogance. We assume animals are dim, but on what evidence? We can’t see inside them any more than they can see inside us.

His motto was ‘What do I know?’

cards.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe … the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
cards.author: Immanuel Kant
cards.source: Critique of Practical Reason, Conclusion (trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott)
cards.more:
Kant opens the conclusion of the Critique of Practical Reason, his 1788 book on ethics, with this. It’s one of the few lyrical moments from a famously dense writer, and probably his most quoted sentence.

The two wonders mirror each other. The night sky shows how tiny we are, one creature on a speck in a huge universe. The moral law shows how big we are: beings who can act on reason and duty instead of impulse. Kant put human dignity in that second fact.

cards.text: Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers to its questions … but rather for the sake of the questions themselves…
cards.author: Bertrand Russell
cards.source: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter 15: The Value of Philosophy (1912)
cards.more:
Bertrand Russell wrote The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers, and this is from the last chapter. He admits philosophy rarely settles anything. Once a question can be answered for sure, it tends to break off and become its own science.

So why bother? Russell says the questions widen your sense of what’s possible and loosen the grip of prejudices you never chose.

cards.text: When we read, another person thinks for us: we merely repeat his mental process.
cards.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
cards.source: On Reading and Books, in Essays of Schopenhauer (trans. Mrs. Rudolf Dircks)
cards.more:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the 19th-century German philosopher best known for his pessimism, was also sharp about reading. The essay goes on to say that someone who reads all day without stopping to think slowly loses the ability to think for himself, the way a man who always rides forgets how to walk.

A slightly awkward thing to find in a feed of quotes.

cards.text: …all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
cards.em: as difficult as they are rare
cards.author: Baruch Spinoza
cards.source: Ethics, Part 5, Proposition 42, Note (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
cards.more:
These are the last words of Spinoza’s Ethics, a book laid out like geometry, with definitions, axioms and proofs. Spinoza argued that freedom comes from understanding. The more clearly we see the causes of our emotions, the less they push us around.

The closing note admits the path is very hard and few take it. Spinoza lived modestly, earning part of his living grinding lenses, and turned down a professorship at Heidelberg, perhaps to protect his freedom to think.

cards.title: The banality of evil
cards.text: At the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt expected a monster. She found a careerist who spoke in clichés and seemed strangely thoughtless.
cards.em: a careerist who spoke in clichés
cards.author: Hannah Arendt
cards.source: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963)
cards.more:
Arendt went to Jerusalem in 1961 to cover the trial for The New Yorker, and her book caused an uproar. Critics said she was excusing Eichmann. She wasn’t. Her point was that he was frighteningly normal: ambitious, obedient and thoughtless rather than demonic.

That moves where we look for danger. If evil needed monsters, most of us could relax. She argued it can come from ordinary people following orders and chasing promotions without asking what their work actually does.

cards.title: Socrates never wrote a word
cards.text: Socrates wrote nothing at all. Most of what we know about him comes from his students Plato and Xenophon, who wrote about him after his death.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Socrates
cards.more:
This creates what scholars call the Socratic problem. How much of ‘Socrates’ is the real man, and how much is Plato putting his own ideas in his teacher’s mouth? Plato’s Socrates and Xenophon’s don’t always sound alike, and the comic playwright Aristophanes mocked yet another version on stage.

In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates even voices a suspicion of writing. A text can’t answer back when you question it, and it can look wise without being wise.

cards.title: A lamp in broad daylight
cards.text: Diogenes the Cynic owned almost nothing and slept in a storage jar in Athens. By day he carried a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being.
cards.author: Diogenes of Sinope
cards.source: Wikipedia: Diogenes
cards.more:
Diogenes lived in the 4th century BC and treated his whole life as a philosophical performance. If the good life means living by nature, he reasoned, most of what society prizes, like wealth, manners and status, is clutter. Later Roman writers turned his jar into a barrel, which is how he’s usually drawn today.

In the most famous story, Alexander the Great visits and asks if he wants anything. Diogenes tells him to stand a little out of his sun.

cards.title: Descartes and the 5 a.m. lessons
cards.text: In 1649 Descartes agreed to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden three times a week at 5 a.m. He caught pneumonia and died in Stockholm in February 1650.
cards.author: René Descartes
cards.source: Wikipedia: René Descartes
cards.more:
By 1649 Descartes was one of the most famous thinkers in Europe, and Christina invited him to set up a scientific academy and teach her his ideas. It went badly. She rejected his mechanical philosophy, he didn’t share her love of ancient Greek, and by mid-January they’d met only four or five times.

Pneumonia is the standard account of his death. Other causes have been floated over the years, including poisoning theories tied to the religious tensions of the time.

cards.title: The ring of invisibility
cards.text: A ring makes you invisible whenever you like, and nobody would ever know what you did. Would you still act exactly as you do now?
cards.author: Plato
cards.source: Republic, Book 2 (trans. Benjamin Jowett)
cards.more:
Glaucon, in Plato’s Republic, says nobody would. He tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seduce a queen, kill a king and seize the throne. People are only just, he argues, because they fear getting caught.

Much of the rest of the Republic is Socrates’ long reply. Justice, he says, is good for the soul in itself, a kind of inner harmony worth having for its own sake.

cards.title: Democritus and the uncuttable bit
cards.text: Around 400 BC, Democritus figured that if you keep cutting matter in half, you eventually hit pieces that can't be cut. He called them atoms, meaning uncuttable.
cards.author: Democritus
cards.source: Known through later ancient writers (c. 5th to 4th century BC); Wikipedia: Democritus
cards.more:
Democritus lived roughly from 460 to 370 BC and built on ideas from the earlier thinker Leucippus. None of his own books survive. We know his views from later writers who quoted him or argued with him.

He had no way to test any of it. It was pure reasoning, and for about two thousand years it stayed that way. This thread follows how the guess finally got real evidence.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Dalton's whole-number clue
cards.text: John Dalton noticed in the early 1800s that carbon and oxygen form two gases. For the same carbon, one has exactly twice the oxygen. Never 1.37 times.
cards.source: Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808); Wikipedia: John Dalton, Law of multiple proportions
cards.more:
The two gases are carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. Dalton's explanation was that each element is made of identical atoms with their own weight, and compounds form when whole atoms join. You can't add half an atom, so the ratios jump in whole steps. His New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808) had the first table of relative atomic weights.

Plenty of scientists still treated atoms as handy bookkeeping. Nobody had seen one. The next clue came from a botanist's microscope.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Pollen that wouldn't sit still
cards.text: In 1827, Robert Brown saw tiny particles from pollen grains jitter nonstop in water. Specks of glass did it too. So did rock dust.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion
cards.more:
Brown was careful. The obvious guess was some life force in the pollen, so he tried particles that had never been alive. They danced the same way, which ruled out biology.

For decades nobody could explain it. People blamed heat currents, vibration or evaporation, but the jiggling never ran down, however still things were kept. The answer came in 1905, and it settled an argument that had lasted since Democritus.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Einstein predicts, Perrin measures
cards.text: Einstein explained the jiggle in 1905: countless water molecules hitting each particle. He predicted how far it should drift. Jean Perrin measured it in 1908. It matched.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion; Nobel Prize in Physics 1926
cards.more:
One molecule is far too small to budge a visible grain. But huge numbers of them hitting from all sides, a little unevenly from moment to moment, add up to a random walk. Einstein's formula tied the size of that wandering to how many molecules a given amount of substance contains.

Perrin's careful experiments with tiny grains won over most of the remaining sceptics. He got the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Shells bouncing off tissue paper
cards.text: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin metal foil in 1909. Most went straight through. About 1 in 8,000 bounced back.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering experiments; Atomic nucleus
cards.more:
Rutherford later compared it to an artillery shell rebounding off tissue paper. In 1911 he worked out why. If an atom's charge and mass were spread evenly, as the leading model said, nothing should bounce back. Only a tiny, dense, positive core could do that.

That core, the nucleus, is tiny. Depending on the element, an atom is roughly 27,000 to 60,000 times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus were a pea, the atom would be a few hundred metres across.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Why can't you walk through walls?
cards.text: Atoms are almost entirely empty space. So when your hand hits a table, why does it stop instead of passing through like two clouds of gnats?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Pauli exclusion principle
cards.more:
Electrons, and a quantum rule about where they can be. The outer parts of atoms are clouds of negatively charged electrons, and those clouds push each other away when atoms get close. What you feel as touch is that push.

Under that is the Pauli exclusion principle, from Wolfgang Pauli in 1925: no two electrons can share the same quantum state, so atoms resist being squeezed. In the late 1960s Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved this is why ordinary matter is stable and takes up room.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.title: Feynman's one-sentence rescue plan
cards.text: If all science were wiped out and one sentence could survive, Richard Feynman would keep this: everything is made of atoms, tiny bits always moving.
cards.author: Richard Feynman
cards.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 1, Atoms in Motion (1963)
cards.more:
His full sentence adds that atoms pull on each other when a little apart and push back when squeezed together. With a bit of imagination, he said, that one idea explains a huge amount, like why water evaporates and what temperature really is.

It also sums up this thread. Democritus guessed it, Dalton used it for chemistry, Brown saw its effects, Einstein and Perrin measured it, and Rutherford found the empty inside held firm by quantum rules.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

cards.text: …there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.
cards.em: the physical phenomena of a candle
cards.author: Michael Faraday
cards.source: The Chemical History of a Candle, Lecture I (1861)
cards.more:
Faraday gave these talks as a course of six lectures for a young audience at the Royal Institution in London, and they were published in 1861. With little more than candles, he showed wax melting into a cup, climbing the wick, turning to vapour and burning into water and carbon dioxide.

Faraday had little formal schooling. He started out as a bookbinder's apprentice, which may be why he was so sure anyone could learn to look at the world this way.

cards.text: …a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Hypothesis, ch. 9, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Henri Poincaré was one of the great mathematicians and physicists of his time, and he thought hard about what scientists actually do. The line before this one says science is built up with facts, as a house is with stones.

His point is that data alone explains nothing. A pile of measurements becomes science when someone finds the pattern that ties it together. Right after this line he adds that, above all, the scientist must foresee.

cards.text: To doubt everything and to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; each saves us from thinking.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Hypothesis, Introduction, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Poincaré wrote this in the introduction to Science and Hypothesis, first published in French in 1902. He was pushing back on two lazy habits. One treats every scientific claim as settled truth. The other waves the whole thing off as arbitrary guesswork.

He wanted readers to sort hypotheses instead. Which ones are necessary, which are handy conventions, and which can be checked by experiment?

cards.text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful.
cards.author: Henri Poincaré
cards.source: Science and Method, Book I, ch. 1, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
cards.more:
Science and Method came out in French in 1908. In this chapter, The Choice of Facts, Poincaré asks how scientists pick what to study when there are endless facts available. His answer, surprising from a hard-headed mathematician, is a sense of beauty.

He means something deeper than colours and surfaces: the harmonious order of the parts. Simple laws that tie many facts together tend to be both beautiful and useful.

cards.text: Science is, I believe, nothing but trained and organized common sense, differing from the latter only as a veteran may differ from a raw recruit
cards.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
cards.source: On the Educational Value of the Natural History Sciences (1854), in Lay Sermons, Addresses and Reviews (1870)
cards.more:
Thomas Henry Huxley, later famous as Darwin's fiercest public defender, gave this talk in 1854 to argue that science belonged in ordinary education. In his view it used the same reasoning everyone uses daily, sharpened by practice and checked more carefully.

So the habits behind it, like noticing, comparing, testing a guess and changing your mind, are open to anyone. The veteran and the recruit have the same kind of brain. One of them has had more training.

cards.title: Earth measured with a shadow
cards.text: On the solstice the noon Sun shone straight down a well at Syene. Alexandria's rods cast a 7.2 degree shadow. So Eratosthenes multiplied the distance by 50.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Eratosthenes
cards.more:
This was in the 3rd century BC. 7.2 degrees is one fiftieth of a circle. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, so on a flat Earth both cities would see the same shadow. The difference shows how much the ground curves between them.

He got around 250,000 stadia. Nobody knows exactly how long his stadion was, but by many estimates he came close to the real 40,000 kilometres. His own book is lost. We know the method through a later writer, Cleomedes.

cards.title: An element found on the Sun
cards.text: During a solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers saw a yellow line in sunlight that matched no known element. Norman Lockyer named it helium, after the Greek for Sun.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Helium
cards.more:
Every element gives off light at its own set of colours, like a barcode. Spread sunlight into a spectrum and those barcodes show up as sharp lines. The new yellow line sat close to two sodium lines, so at first people assumed it was sodium.

Nobody found helium on Earth until 1895, when William Ramsay got it from gas released by a uranium mineral. It's rare here, but it's the second most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen.

cards.title: Marie Curie's two different Nobels
cards.text: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911. Nobody else has won Nobels in two different sciences.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Marie Curie
cards.more:
She was also the first woman to win a Nobel at all. The 1903 prize, shared with her husband Pierre and with Henri Becquerel, was for research on radioactivity, a word she coined. The 1911 prize was hers alone, for discovering polonium and radium. She named polonium after Poland.

Her papers are still radioactive and kept in lead-lined boxes. She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, very likely from years of radiation exposure.

cards.title: Metal that melts in your hand
cards.text: Gallium is a silvery metal that melts at about 29.76 °C, below body temperature. Hold a piece and it slumps into a shiny puddle in your palm.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Gallium
cards.more:
Gallium is one of four metals that are liquid at or near room temperature, along with mercury, caesium and rubidium.

In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for an unknown element he called eka-aluminium, and predicted its properties. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875. Mendeleev had predicted a density of about 5.9 grams per cubic centimetre. The measured value is 5.904.

cards.title: Old church windows aren't melting
cards.text: Old church windows are said to be thicker at the bottom because glass flows. One study found medieval glass flows at most a nanometre in a billion years.
cards.em: a nanometre in a billion years
cards.source: Wikipedia: Glass (Reputed flow)
cards.more:
The lumps were there from the start. Older ways of making flat glass gave ripples and uneven thickness, and smooth float glass only became common in the 1960s.

Glass is an amorphous solid. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but locked in place like a solid's. A 2017 study looked at glass from Westminster Abbey dating to 1268. Even over the age of the universe, any flow at room temperature would be too small to see.

cards.title: Why lakes freeze from the top
cards.text: Most things shrink when they freeze. Water expands by about 9 percent, so ice floats. Lakes freeze top down, and fish get through winter in the water below.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Ice
cards.more:
The cause is hydrogen bonding. In liquid water, molecules tumble past each other and pack fairly close. When water freezes, each molecule locks into an open hexagonal lattice that takes up more room. Ice has a density of about 0.917 grams per cubic centimetre, against roughly 1 for liquid water.

Floating ice insulates the water under it, so lakes rarely freeze solid. Water freezing in cracks also splits rocks. Gallium expands when it solidifies too.

cards.title: Good theories stick their necks out
cards.text: Karl Popper said a theory is scientific if it forbids something, making a risky prediction that could turn out wrong. If nothing could ever refute it, it isn't science.
cards.author: Karl Popper
cards.source: The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934)
cards.more:
Popper noticed a contrast. Einstein's general relativity said exactly how much starlight should bend near the Sun, and the 1919 eclipse could have proved it wrong. Some popular theories of his day seemed able to explain any result at all, which Popper saw as a weakness.

The criterion is called falsifiability. Philosophers still argue about it, and real science is messier than any single rule. As a rough check it still works well.

cards.title: Can a tiny demon beat physics?
cards.text: Maxwell's demon minds a door between two gas boxes. It lets fast molecules through one way, slow ones the other. One side heats up for free. Who pays?
cards.em: One side heats up for free
cards.source: Wikipedia: Maxwell's demon
cards.more:
The demon's memory pays. James Clerk Maxwell posed the puzzle in 1867 to show the second law of thermodynamics is statistical, and it bugged physicists for a century.

To sort molecules, the demon has to measure them and remember the results. In 1929 Leo Szilard linked measurement to entropy. Later, Rolf Landauer and Charles Bennett showed the unavoidable cost is wiping the demon's memory to make room. Erasing information always gives off heat, enough to cancel the gain.

cards.title: Sunlight is 8.3 minutes old
cards.text: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth. So the Sun you see in the sky is the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.
cards.em: as it was eight minutes ago
cards.source: Wikipedia: Sunlight; Speed of light
cards.more:
Light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second in a vacuum. That's about seven and a half laps of Earth every second. The Sun is around 150 million kilometres away, so the trip still takes over eight minutes.

That delay doubles as a ruler. The Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes. This thread climbs the cosmic distance ladder, from our own star to the edge of what we can observe.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: The first distance to a star
cards.text: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel watched 61 Cygni shift as Earth orbited and put it about 10.4 light-years away. No star beyond the Sun had been measured before.
cards.source: Wikipedia: 61 Cygni; Stellar parallax
cards.more:
The modern value is about 11.4. The method is parallax. Hold up a finger and look with one eye, then the other, and it jumps against the background. As Earth swings around its orbit, nearby stars shift against distant ones the same way.

The shift is tiny. For 61 Cygni it's under a third of an arcsecond, smaller than a coin seen from 10 kilometres away. For most of the 20th century, parallax only reached a few hundred light-years.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: 75,000 years to the next star
cards.text: A light-year is about 9.46 trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun is 4.25 light-years away. Voyager 1 would take about 75,000 years to get there.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Light-year; Proxima Centauri; Voyager 1
cards.more:
That star is Proxima Centauri. Voyager 1, one of our fastest spacecraft, moves at roughly 61,000 kilometres per hour, and still needs tens of thousands of years for a trip light makes in just over four.

The Milky Way is close to 90,000 light-years across, with somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars. Parallax can't reach that far. Measuring the galaxy needed a star whose true brightness was known in advance.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Henrietta Leavitt's cosmic yardstick
cards.text: At Harvard in 1908, Henrietta Swan Leavitt noticed that pulsing stars called Cepheids follow a rule: the slower the pulse, the brighter the star.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
cards.more:
Leavitt was one of the women Harvard College Observatory hired as human computers, cataloguing stars from glass photographic plates for 30 cents an hour. She pinned the rule down by 1912, using Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, which are all at roughly the same distance from us.

Time a Cepheid's pulse and you know its real brightness. Compare that with how bright it looks and you get its distance. Leavitt died in 1921, before her yardstick's biggest use.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Andromeda was another galaxy
cards.text: Astronomers in the early 1920s still argued whether the Milky Way was the whole universe. Edwin Hubble found Cepheids in Andromeda and showed it was a separate galaxy.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Andromeda Galaxy
cards.more:
In 1920, Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis held the Great Debate over whether spiral nebulae were clouds inside our galaxy or island universes of their own. Hubble settled it in 1925, using photos from the 100-inch Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson.

Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away. The faint smudge you can see on a dark night is light that left it before our species existed.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Seeing farther than light could travel?
cards.text: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. Yet the edge of the observable universe is about 46.5 billion light-years away. How is that possible?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Observable universe
cards.more:
Space kept stretching while the light was on its way. In the late 1920s, astronomers including Hubble found that distant galaxies move away from us, faster the farther they are. Light from the most distant regions set out when they were much closer.

So 46.5 billion light-years is roughly where those sources are now. The light arrives stretched to redder wavelengths, which is how we measure the expansion. The universe very likely continues past the edge. We just can't get its light.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.title: Earth, smaller than a pixel
cards.text: In 1990 Voyager 1 looked back from over 6 billion kilometres. Earth showed up smaller than a single pixel. Carl Sagan called it a pale blue dot.
cards.author: Carl Sagan
cards.source: Pale Blue Dot (1994); Wikipedia: Pale Blue Dot
cards.more:
Sagan was one of those who pushed for the shot. It was taken on February 14, 1990, as part of a Family Portrait of the solar system. Soon after, Voyager 1's cameras were switched off for good to save power. Earth fills about 0.12 of a pixel, caught in a streak of scattered sunlight.

Sagan's argument was that all our history and quarrels happen on one small, fragile world. This thread started with sunlight eight minutes old and ends here.

thread.title: How big is the universe? (7 cards)

cards.text: …the surface of the Moon is not perfectly smooth … full of hollows and protuberances, just like the surface of the Earth itself
cards.author: Galileo Galilei
cards.source: The Sidereal Messenger (1610), trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (1880)
cards.more:
Galileo didn't invent the telescope, but he built better ones and pointed them at the sky. Through one that made the Moon look about thirty times wider, he saw bright points appear in the dark part, then grow and join the lit side. Mountain peaks catching the sunrise.

The old view held that heavenly bodies were perfect spheres. Sidereus Nuncius came out on March 13, 1610, the first scientific work based on observations through a telescope.

cards.text: …the Galaxy is nothing else but a mass of innumerable stars planted together in clusters. … a vast crowd of stars presents itself to view
cards.author: Galileo Galilei
cards.source: The Sidereal Messenger (1610), trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (1880)
cards.more:
For all of human history, the Milky Way had been a soft band of light across the sky, and philosophers argued about what it was. Galileo's small telescope settled it at a glance. The glow was stars too faint and too crowded for the naked eye to separate.

It took three more centuries to learn that the Milky Way is a disc-shaped galaxy with us inside it, one of a great many.

cards.text: This whole earth which we inhabit is but a point in space. … Why should I feel lonely? is not our planet in the Milky Way?
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 5, Solitude (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau lived alone in a small cabin by Walden Pond in Massachusetts from 1845 to 1847. People kept asking if he got lonely out there, especially on rainy and snowy nights. This was his answer.

Next to the distances between stars, the walk from his cabin to town is nothing. Loneliness, he goes on to say, isn't measured in miles at all.

cards.text: …it's not improbable that the rest of the Planets have their Dress and Furniture, and perhaps their Inhabitants too as well as this Earth of ours
cards.author: Christiaan Huygens
cards.source: The Celestial Worlds Discover'd, Book I (English trans., 1698)
cards.more:
Christiaan Huygens ground his own telescope lenses and found Saturn's largest moon, Titan. He was also first to explain Saturn's odd look as a thin, flat ring. He finished this book, Cosmotheoros in Latin, shortly before he died in 1695, and arranged for it to come out after his death.

His logic follows from Copernicus. If Earth is one planet among several, why should it be the only one with life? We've now found thousands of planets around other stars and still can't say.

cards.text: …to declare that this glorious science is not the grinning mathematical skeleton that it has been represented to be.
cards.author: Garrett P. Serviss
cards.source: Astronomy with an Opera-glass, Introduction (1888)
cards.more:
Garrett Serviss was an American journalist who wanted ordinary people to fall for the sky. For this book he surveyed the constellations visible from New York using only an opera glass, and promised he described nothing he hadn't seen himself.

He opens with a funny story. When Venus blazed in the evening sky in 1887, some New Yorkers decided it was an electric balloon Thomas Edison sent up every night.

cards.title: A teaspoon worth 900 pyramids
cards.text: A neutron star squeezes about 1.4 Suns into a ball roughly 20 kilometres across. A teaspoon of it has the mass of around 900 Great Pyramids.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Neutron star
cards.more:
That teaspoon would be over 5.5 trillion kilograms. Neutron stars are what's left after some massive stars explode as supernovae. The core collapses so hard that its matter is crushed into mostly neutrons, packed as tight as an atomic nucleus.

The collapse spins them up, so newborn ones can turn several hundred times a second. Some sweep beams of radiation past Earth like lighthouses. These pulsars were first found by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in 1967.

cards.title: A day longer than a year
cards.text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west.
cards.em: the Sun rises in the west
cards.source: Wikipedia: Venus
cards.more:
Because it spins slowly backwards while orbiting, one sunrise to the next takes about 117 Earth days. That's shorter than its rotation, but still long.

The view would be grim. A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect and keeps the surface around 464 °C. That's hotter than Mercury, even though Venus is nearly twice as far from the Sun. It's almost the size of Earth.

cards.title: A full light-day from home
cards.text: By November 2026, Voyager 1 was expected to be one light-day from Earth. A radio message to it takes a full day to arrive. It launched in 1977.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Voyager 1
cards.more:
Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and kept going. On August 25, 2012, it crossed the heliopause, where the Sun's wind of charged particles gives way to the thin gas between stars. It's the most distant human-made object.

It carries the Golden Record, a gold-plated disc of sounds, music and images from Earth. Its power is fading, and engineers keep switching instruments off to keep it talking.

cards.title: A volcano the size of Italy
cards.text: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 21 kilometres high, two and a half Everests. It's about 600 kilometres wide, covering some 300,000 square kilometres. That's roughly Italy.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Olympus Mons
cards.more:
Olympus Mons is a shield volcano, built from countless flows of runny lava, like Hawaii's volcanoes but far bigger. Mars has no moving tectonic plates. On Earth, plates slide over volcanic hotspots and spread eruptions into island chains. On Mars the crust sits still over the hotspot, so one volcano keeps growing.

Its only real rival is Rheasilvia, a central peak on the asteroid Vesta, roughly tied with it as the tallest mountain yet found in the solar system.

cards.title: The Sun is almost everything
cards.text: The Sun holds 99.86 percent of the solar system's mass. Jupiter and Saturn make up nearly 90 percent of the rest. Everything else, Earth included, is crumbs.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Solar System; Sun
cards.more:
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a dense part of a gas cloud collapsed. Most of the material fell to the centre, and the planets formed from the thin disc of leftovers spinning around it.

In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, turning more than four billion kilograms of matter into energy every second, as Einstein's E = mc² describes. It's still only about halfway through its stable, hydrogen-burning life.

cards.title: Moving the Sun to the centre
cards.text: Nicolaus Copernicus made Earth one of several planets circling the Sun. The odd backward loops planets make in our sky are just us watching from a moving platform.
cards.author: Nicolaus Copernicus
cards.source: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543)
cards.more:
In his model Earth also spins daily on its axis. The idea wasn't brand new. The ancient Greek astronomer Aristarchus had suggested a Sun-centred system centuries earlier. Copernicus worked it out in mathematical detail, and his book appeared in 1543, the year he died. A well-known story says he was handed a printed copy on his deathbed.

His model still used perfect circles, so it didn't match the planets exactly. It took Kepler's ellipses and Galileo's telescope to make it hard to deny.

cards.title: Kepler refused to fudge Mars
cards.text: Johannes Kepler's best circle for Mars missed Tycho Brahe's observations by just eight minutes of arc. Kepler wouldn't ignore the gap. It led him to the ellipse.
cards.author: Johannes Kepler
cards.source: Astronomia nova (1609)
cards.more:
Eight minutes of arc is about a quarter of the Moon's apparent width. Tycho Brahe had spent decades making the most precise naked-eye measurements of the planets ever recorded, and the gap was bigger than his error. Kepler wrote that those eight minutes alone would lead to the reform of all of astronomy.

He published his laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1621. Decades later, Isaac Newton showed that gravity explains all three.

cards.title: Where is everybody?
cards.text: Our galaxy has 100 to 400 billion stars, many older than the Sun. If a tiny fraction grew civilisations that travel between stars, why haven't we seen any?
cards.source: Wikipedia: Fermi paradox; Milky Way
cards.more:
Nobody knows yet. The puzzle is named after physicist Enrico Fermi, who in 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, asked something like: where is everybody?

There are many candidate answers. Maybe life is common but intelligence is rare. Maybe civilisations destroy themselves or stay home. Maybe they're too far apart in space and time, or signal in ways we haven't thought to look for. Or maybe we really are alone.

cards.title: Health and money don’t count
cards.text: The Stoics said only one thing is truly good: a good character. Money, health and status are ‘indifferents’. Nice to have, but a crook can have them too.
cards.em: only one thing is truly good
cards.author: Zeno of Citium
cards.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 7
cards.more:
Zeno of Citium started teaching this in a painted colonnade in Athens around 300 BC. He split the world in three: good (a good character), bad (a bad character) and everything else.

The Stoics admitted some indifferents are ‘preferred’. Health beats sickness, and you’re allowed to go after it. But no outside thing can make you a good person or stop you being one. So for a Stoic, a missed promotion can’t hurt you. Cheating to get one can.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. … Not in our power are the body, property, reputation … whatever are not our own acts.
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 1 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
This is the first line of the Encheiridion, or ‘handbook’, a short summary of Epictetus’s teaching put together by his student Arrian. He sorts everything into two piles. Your judgments, intentions and desires are yours. Your body, your money and what people think of you are finally up to the world.

Most daily stress comes from mixing up the piles, like trying to control someone’s opinion of you while ignoring your own response to it.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible…
cards.em: by the opinions about the things
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 5 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
Epictetus splits every upset into two steps. Something happens, then you add a story about it. This is a disaster. That was an insult. Most of the suffering lives in the story.

Pain is still real for him. But there’s more room than you’d think between what happens and how you take it. Cognitive behavioural therapy grew partly out of the same idea, and its founders credited the Stoics.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: …nothing ought to be unexpected by us. … we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 91 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1920)
cards.more:
Seneca wrote this after a fire destroyed the city of Lyon in a single night, leaving a friend of his badly shaken. His advice became a Stoic exercise later called premeditatio malorum, rehearsing in your head what could go wrong.

Oddly, the goal is calm. If you’ve already pictured losing a job or a plan falling apart, the real thing finds you ready. And picturing the loss reminds you what you have now.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: …wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
cards.author: Epictetus
cards.source: Encheiridion, 8 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
Epictetus isn’t telling you to stop trying. Work for the outcome you want. But once the result is in, arguing with it only adds a second injury to the first.

‘Tranquil flow of life’ echoes an old Stoic definition of happiness: a life that flows smoothly, like a river going around rocks. Centuries later Nietzsche praised a similar attitude and called it amor fati, love of fate.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.title: Pull your circles closer
cards.text: Hierocles pictured you at the centre of rings: family, relatives, neighbours, city, all humanity. His exercise was to keep pulling the outer rings inward.
cards.author: Hierocles
cards.source: Hierocles, Elements of Ethics (fragment preserved by Stobaeus)
cards.more:
Hierocles was a Stoic of the 2nd century AD, and he shows the side of Stoicism people forget. If virtue is the only good, then justice and kindness to others sit at the core. The Stoics called themselves citizens of the world.

The circles make that practical. Nobody has to love all humanity in the abstract. You just move each ring one step closer. A cousin gets treated a bit more like a sibling, a stranger a bit more like a neighbour.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: …to inquire of his spirit: “What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?”
cards.em: in what respect are you better?
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: On Anger, Book 3.36 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1889)
cards.more:
Seneca borrowed this nightly review from the philosopher Quintus Sextius and says he does it himself. When the lamp is out, he goes over his whole day, what he said and what he did, hiding nothing from himself.

It’s where the rest of this thread becomes a habit. Each night you check where you mixed up what you control with what you don’t. Seneca says the sleep that follows is sweeter.

thread.title: Stoicism in 7 cards

cards.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
cards.em: I shall meet with the busybody
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 2.1 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire, and this is how he got ready for a workday. The passage goes on: these people are his kin, made for cooperation like feet, hands and eyelids, so they can’t harm him and he can’t hate them.

He pairs two ideas. Expect friction, so it doesn’t catch you off guard. And people who behave badly usually can’t see what’s good, which makes them easier to pity than to hate.

cards.text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 10.16 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
By Book 10 of the Meditations, Marcus sounds fed up with himself. He’d studied with the best teachers and could describe the good life in detail. This line is him cutting off his own stalling.
