Talking about virtue can feel like progress, which makes it a comfy place to hide. Marcus’s fix is three words long: but be such.

cards.text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. … so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
Seneca opens the first of his 124 surviving letters to his friend Lucilius with this, written near the end of his life. He notices how carefully we guard money and possessions while letting others spend our hours freely. Nobody feels in debt for having taken someone’s time.

The letters were his way of teaching philosophy as a chat between friends. Nearly 2,000 years later, meetings and feeds are still ousting us from possession.

cards.text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
The letter went to a friend bracing for trouble. Many of the disasters we dread never arrive, and the ones that do rarely look how we pictured them. Meanwhile the worrying is already real suffering.

In the same letter he sorts fears into three kinds. Some things torment us more than they should, some before they should, and some when they never should at all.

cards.text: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny … To follow I am ready. If I choose not, I make myself a wretch, and still must follow.
cards.author: Cleanthes
cards.source: Quoted in Epictetus, Encheiridion, 52 (trans. George Long, 1877)
cards.more:
Cleanthes ran the Stoic school after Zeno. He’d been a boxer and paid for his studies by carrying water at night. Epictetus loved these lines enough to put them near the end of his handbook, and Seneca turned them into Latin with an extra line: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.

In the poem the road goes where it goes either way. The only choice left is whether you walk it or get dragged.

cards.title: The view from above
cards.text: One habit of Marcus Aurelius: picture the earth from high above, crowded with people being born, quarrelling and dying, then find your own problem down there.
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 9.30 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
Marcus comes back to this image again and again in the Meditations: crowds, voyages, feasts and quarrels, plus everyone in the past and future who’ll never know your name. The historian Pierre Hadot called it ‘the view from above’.

The point is proportion. An awkward email or a rival’s win looks tiny from high enough up, and so does the craving for praise. How you treat people still looks the same size.

cards.title: Philosophy is for women too
cards.text: In first-century Rome, Musonius Rufus argued women should study philosophy just like men. They have the same reason, he said, and the same natural pull toward virtue.
cards.author: Musonius Rufus
cards.source: Lectures, 3: That Women Too Should Study Philosophy
cards.more:
Musonius Rufus was one of the most respected teachers in imperial Rome, and he taught Epictetus. His lectures survive in notes his students took. Two of them argue that women should study philosophy and that daughters deserve the same education as sons, a striking view for the time.

His reasoning is very Stoic. If a good life depends on reason and character, not status or the body, then everyone has what it takes. He also insisted philosophy was something you practise.

cards.title: The obstacle is the way
cards.text: Ryan Holiday built a whole 2014 book on one line from Marcus Aurelius: the mind turns whatever blocks it into material to work with.
cards.author: Ryan Holiday
cards.source: The Obstacle Is the Way (2014), drawing on Meditations, Book 5.20
cards.more:
In Book 5 of the Meditations, Marcus notes that other people can block his actions but not his attitude. The mind turns each hindrance into an aid, so the obstacle on the road helps us along the road.

Holiday’s book retells this through stories of athletes, generals and entrepreneurs, and it helped kick off the modern Stoicism revival. Its practical question: what does this obstacle let me practise? A harsh critic, for example, is a chance at patience.

cards.title: Philosophy as mental drills
cards.text: Pierre Hadot argued that ancient philosophy was a training programme for the mind more than a set of theories. Stoic texts are full of repeated drills.
cards.em: a training programme for the mind
cards.author: Pierre Hadot
cards.source: Philosophy as a Way of Life (1995)
cards.more:
Hadot, a French scholar of ancient thought, noticed something odd about the Meditations. Marcus repeats himself constantly. Hadot’s explanation: Marcus was writing spiritual exercises for himself, notes to reshape his own habits of thought, the way an athlete repeats drills.

Seen that way, the repetition is the point. Understanding a Stoic idea once is easy. Living by it takes the same rehearsal as any other skill.

cards.title: Stoicism started with a shipwreck
cards.text: Zeno of Citium, a merchant, survived a shipwreck on the way to Athens. Around 301 BC he started teaching in the Painted Porch, the Stoa Poikile. Hence ‘Stoics’.
cards.author: Zeno of Citium
cards.source: Wikipedia: Zeno of Citium
cards.more:
The story comes from Diogenes Laërtius, an ancient biographer, so some details may be embellished. In Athens, Zeno read about Socrates in a bookshop and asked where to find men like that. The bookseller reportedly pointed at Crates the Cynic, who happened to be walking past. Zeno became his student before founding his own school.

His followers were first called Zenonians. The name that stuck came from the porch, a painted colonnade in the Athenian marketplace.

cards.title: Meditations was never meant for us
cards.text: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations as private notes he never meant to publish. One old manuscript calls it ‘to himself’. Parts were written on campaign along the Danube.
cards.em: notes he never meant to publish
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Wikipedia: Meditations
cards.more:
Marcus was emperor from 161 to 180 AD, and wrote in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans. Notes in the text place Book 1 among the Quadi, a tribe he was fighting near the River Hron in modern Slovakia, and Book 2 at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube.

So it reads less like a guru’s lecture and more like a tired, busy man reminding himself how he wants to behave.

cards.title: Epictetus in a prison camp
cards.text: US pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam in 1965 and held for over seven years. He credited Epictetus, a former slave, with getting him through.
cards.author: James Stockdale
cards.source: Wikipedia: James Stockdale
cards.more:
Stockdale was the most senior naval officer held in Hanoi, in the prison Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. He got the Medal of Honor in 1976 for his leadership as a prisoner, and later spent years at Stanford’s Hoover Institution writing and lecturing on Stoicism.

His essay Courage Under Fire: Testing Epictetus’s Doctrines in a Laboratory of Human Behavior spells it out. His captors controlled his body and his circumstances. His judgments and his will stayed his.

cards.title: What would you still have?
cards.text: Say a fire takes everything tonight: house, things, savings. List what you’d still have. Is that list where most of your attention goes?
cards.author: Seneca
cards.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
cards.more:
Seneca’s answer: your character and your judgment, the things no fire can touch. He tells the story of Stilbo, a philosopher whose city was captured and whose wife and children were lost. When the conquering general Demetrius asked if he’d lost anything, Stilbo said he had all his goods with him.

He meant the things no army could carry off. The Stoics didn’t pretend losses don’t hurt. They just wanted to know what a person actually depends on.

cards.title: Have you done it too?
cards.text: Think of the last person who really annoyed you. Be honest: have you ever done something similar, or wanted to?
cards.em: have you ever done something similar
cards.author: Marcus Aurelius
cards.source: Meditations, Book 11.18 (trans. George Long, 1862)
cards.more:
Marcus Aurelius assumed the answer is usually yes. In Book 11 he lists ways to cool down when someone offends him. One is to remember that you do plenty wrong too, and are a person like others. Even when you avoid a fault, he says, you often have the urge and are held back only by caution or worry about your reputation.

Most anger quietly treats the other person as a different kind of creature. Remembering your own slips brings them back to human size.

cards.title: Sanskrit, Greek and Latin are cousins
cards.text: In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, said Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were too alike to be a coincidence. They must share a lost ancestor.
cards.em: too alike to be a coincidence
cards.source: William Jones, Third Anniversary Discourse to the Asiatic Society (1786); Wikipedia, William Jones (philologist)
cards.more:
That lost source is now called Proto-Indo-European. Nobody ever wrote it down. It was spoken roughly five or six thousand years ago and has been rebuilt by comparing its descendants.

Jones thought Gothic, Celtic and Persian came from it too, though he also wrongly lumped in Egyptian and Japanese. The family now covers most languages of Europe, Iran and northern India, from Hindi to Welsh to English. Nearly half the world's people speak one natively.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: Why father sounds like pater
cards.text: Latin pater, English father. Latin pes, English foot. Latin tres, English three. Where Latin kept an old p or t, Germanic languages shifted it to f or th.
cards.em: shifted it to f or th
cards.source: Jacob Grimm, Deutsche Grammatik (1822); Wikipedia, Grimm's law
cards.more:
Rasmus Rask spotted the pattern, and Jacob Grimm, of the fairy tales, laid it out in 1822. It's now called Grimm's law. P became f, t became th, k became h, probably in the first millennium BC.

It explains pairs like Latin cornu and English horn, or piscis and fish. It's also why English has native words next to later Latin borrowings, like father and paternal, foot and pedal. Sound change turned out to follow rules.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: English arrived by boat
cards.text: English wasn't born in England. Angles, Saxons and their neighbours brought it across the North Sea in the mid-5th century.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Old English; Beowulf
cards.more:
The name is a souvenir of the trip. English comes from the Angles, and England was once Englaland, land of the Angles.

Old English had grammar endings much like modern German, and letters we've lost, like thorn and ash. Beowulf opens with Hwaet, and needs translating today. Its only manuscript was copied around 975 to 1025 and nearly burned in a library fire in 1731. Britain's Celtic languages left few words, mostly place and river names like Thames and Avon.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: The Vikings gave us they
cards.text: Viking settlers gave English some of its most basic words: they, them and their, plus egg, knife and sky. Window comes from Old Norse vindauga, literally wind-eye.
cards.source: Wikipedia, List of English words of Old Norse origin (citing the Online Etymology Dictionary)
cards.more:
Sky meant cloud in Old Norse. Norse speakers settled in northern and eastern England from the 9th to the 11th centuries, in the Danelaw, and the two languages were close enough that neighbours could probably get the gist.

Borrowing nouns is common. Borrowing pronouns is rare, and shows how closely the two groups mixed. Some scholars think the mixing helped English drop many grammar endings and lean on word order instead.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.text: …when the brute lives, and is in the charge of a Saxon slave, she goes by her Saxon name; but becomes a Norman, and is called pork…
cards.author: Walter Scott
cards.source: Ivanhoe, ch. 1 (1819)
cards.more:
Wamba the jester is explaining to Gurth the swineherd how the Norman Conquest of 1066 split English. Animals tended by English peasants kept Old English names: swine, cow, sheep, calf. The meat served to French-speaking lords got French ones: pork, beef, mutton, veal.

Scott was a novelist, and the real story is messier, but the pattern holds. Everyday words tend to be Germanic. Words for law, government and food often came through French, like commence next to begin.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: Bite used to sound like beet
cards.text: Between about 1400 and 1700, English long vowels moved. Bite once sounded roughly like beet, and house like hoose. Spelling settled while the sounds were still moving.
cards.source: Wikipedia, Great Vowel Shift
cards.more:
This is the Great Vowel Shift, and it's the main reason English vowel letters act so oddly next to Spanish, Italian or German, where a written i still sounds like ee. Chaucer said name with a vowel like the a in father.

Nobody fully knows why it happened. Theories include social mixing after the Black Death and London blending regional accents. Early printers, some of them Flemish, fixed spellings that stuck long after the sounds changed.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.text: …sounds are too volatile and subtile for legal restraints; to enchain syllables, and to lash the wind, are equally the undertakings of pride…
cards.author: Samuel Johnson
cards.source: Preface to A Dictionary of the English Language (1755)
cards.more:
Johnson spent 1746 to 1755 on his Dictionary, with a few clerks to copy out quotations. He started half hoping to fix English in place, the way the French Academy tried to guard French. By the end he'd given up. Language can be recorded but not frozen.

English had already been through Germanic settlers, Viking pronouns, Norman vocabulary and a vowel shift. It never stopped moving, and every new slang word is part of the same story.

thread.title: How English became English (7 cards)

cards.title: Nice used to be an insult
cards.text: Nice comes, through Old French, from Latin nescius, ignorant. In medieval English, calling someone nice meant they were foolish or simple. Pleasant came much later.
cards.em: meant they were foolish or simple
cards.source: Wiktionary, nice (etymology); Online Etymology Dictionary, nice
cards.more:
The Latin root is ne, not, plus scire, to know, the same scire behind science. Over the centuries nice drifted through shy, fussy and precise. In Shakespeare's time it often meant precise, which survives in a nice distinction. The pleasant meaning took over in the 1700s.

Linguists call that kind of upgrade amelioration. The reverse happened to silly, which once meant blessed or happy, and to awful, which meant full of awe.

cards.title: Your muscles are little mice
cards.text: Muscle comes from Latin musculus, little mouse. Romans thought a flexing muscle, especially a bicep, looked like a small mouse moving under the skin.
cards.source: Wiktionary, muscle (etymology), from Latin musculus, diminutive of mus, mouse
cards.more:
Greek used one word, mys, for both mouse and muscle, and several other languages make the same link. Mus, mouse, is an old Indo-European root, related to English mouse itself.

Musculus also meant mussel, the shellfish, probably because the dark shell looked mouse-like too. So anyone at the gym showing off their muscles is, going by the Latin, showing off their mice.

cards.text: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested...
cards.author: Francis Bacon
cards.source: Essays, Of Studies (1625 edition)
cards.more:
Bacon explains the metaphor straight after. Some books you dip into, some you read without much care, and a few you read wholly, with diligence and attention. Some can even be read by deputy, through someone else's summary.

The same short essay has another famous line: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.

cards.text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences…
cards.author: William Strunk Jr.
cards.source: The Elements of Style, rule 13, Omit needless words (1918)
cards.more:
The sentence goes on: for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts. William Strunk taught English at Cornell and privately printed this guide for his students. One of them, E. B. White, later revised it into a bestseller.

Strunk added that sentences can still be long and full of detail, as long as every word tells.

cards.text: Books are the treasured wealth of the world and the fit inheritance of generations and nations.
cards.em: the treasured wealth of the world
cards.author: Henry David Thoreau
cards.source: Walden, ch. 3, Reading (1854)
cards.more:
Thoreau wrote this in his cabin at Walden Pond, where he lived from 1845 to 1847, cutting life down to essentials. The classics were among the few things he kept.

The chapter is demanding. He says most people only read easy books and never learn reading in the higher sense, the kind you stand on tiptoe for. He wanted people tackling Homer and Aeschylus, ideally in the original.

cards.text: The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid.
cards.author: Jane Austen
cards.source: Northanger Abbey, ch. 14 (1817)
cards.more:
Henry Tilney says this to Catherine Morland, who expected a clever young man to look down on novels. Many people did. Novels were seen as frivolous, especially for young women.

Austen didn't agree. Earlier in the book she steps out of the story to defend novels as works in which the greatest powers of the mind are displayed. Northanger Abbey was written in the late 1790s and published only after her death.

cards.text: No man but a blockhead ever wrote, except for money.
cards.author: Samuel Johnson
cards.source: James Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson, entry for 1776 (1791)
cards.more:
Johnson really said it, according to his friend and biographer James Boswell, who wrote down his talk as it happened. Boswell pushed back right away, calling it a strange opinion and pointing to plenty of counterexamples.

Johnson knew the subject. He grew up poor, arrived in London nearly penniless and wrote for hire for years. Essays, reviews, parliamentary reports, a whole dictionary.

cards.text: The etymologist finds the deadest word to have been once a brilliant picture. Language is fossil poetry.
cards.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
cards.source: Essays: Second Series, The Poet (1844)
cards.more:
Emerson means every word started as someone's fresh image, and heavy use wore the image away. Limestone works the same way, made of tiny shells that no longer look like shells.

Etymology cracks the stone open. Muscle was a little mouse. Window was a wind-eye. Disaster is a bad star, from when bad luck was blamed on the planets. Daisy is the day's eye, because it opens in the morning.

cards.title: Why experts write badly
cards.text: Steven Pinker blames most hard-to-read writing on the curse of knowledge. Once you know something, you forget what not knowing felt like, so you skip steps.
cards.author: Steven Pinker
cards.source: The Sense of Style, ch. 3 (2014)
cards.more:
Psychologists see it in experiments. In one, people tapping out a tune expected listeners to name it far more often than they could, because the tappers heard the melody in their heads.

Pinker says picturing your reader isn't enough, since the curse makes that hard. He suggests showing drafts to real people, and rereading your own work once you've partly forgotten it. His picture of good writing is helping a smart friend see something.

cards.title: Bad writing hides bad thinking
cards.text: George Orwell argued sloppy language and sloppy thought feed each other. Stale phrases let writers avoid deciding what they mean, and politicians make ugly things sound bloodless.
cards.author: George Orwell
cards.source: Politics and the English Language (1946)
cards.more:
His examples were political. Bombing villages and driving out the people who lived there could be described in a technical-sounding phrase that spared readers any picture of what happened. Euphemism, he thought, defends the indefensible.

He gave six rules, all versions of one instinct: use a short, plain word where a long or ready-made one tempts you, and prefer the active voice. The last rule was an escape hatch. Break any of the others rather than write something ugly.

cards.title: Read a lot, write a lot
cards.text: There's no shortcut to writing well, says Stephen King. Read a lot, write a lot. Bad books teach you as much as good ones.
cards.em: Read a lot, write a lot
cards.author: Stephen King
cards.source: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft (2000)
cards.more:
On Writing is half memoir, half manual. King finished it after a van hit him in 1999 and nearly killed him. He reads in waiting rooms, at meals and on the treadmill, and says a writer too busy to read has given up the main tool of the trade.

He's also suspicious of adverbs. If he answered angrily needs the angrily, the dialogue probably isn't doing its job. He'd rather fix the sentence than prop it up.

cards.title: Who put the b in debt?
cards.text: Nobody pronounces the b in debt, and for centuries nobody wrote it either. So where did it come from?
cards.em: Nobody pronounces the b in debt
cards.source: Wiktionary, debt (etymology)
cards.more:
Scholars added it on purpose. English took the word from Old French dette, and Middle English spelled it dette or det, the way it sounded. Renaissance writers who admired Latin then slipped in a b to show its root, debitum, what is owed.

The same fashion gave doubt its b and receipt its p. Some were mistakes. Island got its s by wrong analogy with isle, though it's native English, from Old English igland.

cards.title: Where did OK come from?
cards.text: OK may be the most widely understood word on Earth. It first appeared in a Boston newspaper in 1839. What did the two letters stand for?
cards.em: most widely understood word on Earth
cards.source: Wikipedia, OK (citing Allen Walker Read's studies)
cards.more:
Oll korrect, a deliberate misspelling of all correct. In the late 1830s Boston papers had a fad for jokey abbreviations of misspelled phrases. Almost all of them died. The linguist Allen Walker Read traced OK to the Boston Morning Post of 23 March 1839.

The 1840 election saved it. Democrats said it stood for Old Kinderhook, the nickname of President Martin Van Buren, who came from Kinderhook, New York. Vote for OK caught on, and the word went national.
